subtopic: EXTENSION OF SUPPORT PRICES TO JULY 31, 1949
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a statement that will be of interest to the producers of oats and barley. During the current crop season support prices for both oats and barley are in effect and the government intends to extend these to July 31, 1949, at the same support levels prevailing this crop year. Oats will continue to be supported at levels based on 611 cents for No. 1 feed oats, in store Fort William-Port Arthur, with other grades at appropriate differentials to be fixed from time to time by the wheat board. Barley will also be supported at 90 cents per bushel for No. 1 feed barley, in store Fort William-Port Arthur, with other grades at appropriate differentials to be fixed from time to time by the wheat board.
The purpose in making this announcement at this time is to enable producers of oats and barley to plan their operations for the coming crop year with the assurance that market prices will not decline below the support levels. As in the present crop year, the Canadian wheat board will be directed to implement this policy.

speechtext:
Hon. MILTON F. GREGG (Minister of Veterans Affairs): I promised to investigate and report on the Veterans Land Act Braefoot project in British Columbia.
A committee was appointed, comprising Mr. R. W. Wallace, a technical expert in housing values, who was suggested to us by Mr. J. L. E. Price, chairman of the Canadian Legion housing committee. Mr. Wallace was selected because of his knowledge of values set on similar projects throughout the dominion and because of his knowledge of construction standards elsewhere.
The other two members of the committee were selected because of their intimate knowledge of local conditions and prevailing values on Vancouver island. They were Mr. Fred N. Cabeldu, who operates an insurance agency, and Mr. Brooke Stephenson, a member of the firm of Kerr and Stephenson, real estate, mortgage and insurance. Both these two British Columbia gentlemen are veterans.
It was felt that an impartial valuation could be reached by employing a committee of this kind. As a result of their inspection, it was found that in the case of twenty houses a slightly higher valuation was set, whilst with respect to the remaining eight, it was their opinion that a reduction should be made. I can assure this house that the valuation by this committee was absolutely impartial and uninfluenced by my department.
Where higher values were set than the price placed upon the property I do not propose any increase, and where lower values have been set I propose to take the committee's advice and make a reduction accordingly.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak for two reasons: first, to ask for a better understanding between the farmer and the consumer, and second, to put the case of the farmer and livestock producer for a better deal in the matter of prices.
The consumer, for the most part, knows very little about the cost of food production. He also thinks that because he pays high prices for food the farmer must be getting rich from the sale of his products. The farmer is not getting much more now than he did in 1940, although the price of most foods has doubled. For instance, in 1940 a can of tomatoes sold for eight and a half cents, from which the grower received two cents per can. Tomatoes now sell at twenty-five cents per can but the grower receives only three and. three-quarter cents per can. In other words, while the price of a can of
The Address

Mr. Aylesworth

tomatoes has risen sixteen and a half cents per tin, the added return to the farmer is only one and three-quarter cents. The overworked farmer, with his long hours, has always given the Canadian people good value for their money, even though by the middle of the war most of the young men from the farms had gone into factories for higher pay and better hours and the farmer had to get more money to buy machines to replace the men and pay very much higher wages. The consumer must also realize that the farmer is suffering under 'the burden of high prices just as much as the city dweller. The prices of his feeds, his seeds, his fertilizer and all those things required to turn out food have gone away up, as well as the clothing and so forth which also he has to buy.
Canadians must be informed that it is not the farmer who is responsible for the increased cost of living; it is the spread between the producer and the consumer over which the farmer has no control that has helped to cause these high prices. Of course the farmer has to have more for his produce in order to meet the higher demands on his purse for that which he must buy, but, as a Canadian farmer, I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that the farmer is not looking for more money than will give him a fair living and allow him to maintain his farm and provide for his old age. This is right, for nobody in this country earns his bread in a harder way than does the farmer.
There is a great deal of pressure on the government from certain groups for the return of price control on food. The farmer suffered from controls the most during the war, because food was the first thing on which controls were imposed. As it was his war contribution he dad not complain, but he does not want to see the return of controls now. Following the war we had price control on farm products until very recently. The terms of British food contracts have kept the price of farm products below the world level, so controls are not the answer. In spite of controls, production in Canada is down. During the war the government oversold the value of controls. As soon as controls are applied1 in one place the pressure bursts out somewhere else. In peace you cannot pick out one control, such as price control, and try to enforce it without setting up controls on all things. After every war, prices are at a high level because of war waste, lessening of production in farm products and other things on account of the shortage of manpower, and because of the limited production of consumer goods during the war.

The end of the war brings forth demands for production as great as in war years, but the urge to increase production and stop spending is missing. The Minister of Finance has tried to control our spending by putting a twenty-five per cent tax on a lot of things, although he frankly admitted that the government does not need the money. They tax cars, but they forget that many workers must have cars to get to and from work, because of the housing shortage which forces them to live miles from their place of employment.
The minister warned industry against taking heavy profits while his government is rolling up a three-quarter billion dollar surplus. The government could very well now remove many of the hidden taxes that do so much to keep the cost of food high. For instance, there is the eight per cent sales tax on which the government collected $328 million last year. They could give income tax relief to the small-salaried man and the white collar worker. These people have no bargaining agents and are hit hard by high taxes. Increase the income tax exemptions to $2,500 for married men and $1,500 for single men. I hope the people of Canada realize that when the cost of an article is doubled the cost of their tax on that article is also doubled.
The farmer had a right to expect a fair price for his meat and cheese in the food contracts with Great Britain, but he finds that they are still much below the prices in the open world market, and he knows now that the only reason that any increase was given in the price, 'and perhaps the reason that only wheat was included in the agreements, was that in order to get wheat at a very low price Britain had to agree to take the meat and cheese at a higher figure. The prices provided in the new agreement are just high enough to force prices up on the home market, but in no case are they enough to repay the farmer for the rise in feed, labour and consumer goods costs. It only raised the cost of living for Canadians without giving any assistance to the farmer. During the war we supplied meat and cheese, along with wheat, for the United Kingdom agreements at a price very much below world prices, on the assurance of the Minister of Agriculture that for many years to come we would enjoy this privilege.
On February 28 last year the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) as reported at page 933 of Hansard, said:
Naturally I raised the question which is in the mind of ranchers rand others who are producing cattle across Canada. I asked how long were we likely to have a market in Great Britain of the same proportions as we have it

The Address-Mr. Aylesworth
now. The reply I received was that there would be a general shortage for a considerable time. They did mention a term of years. I hesitate to mention a term of years to the committee tonight, because I do not know that it was given to me with the idea of mentioning it or making them responsible for any particular figure; for, just as some say, that I guess wrong sometimes, I suppose ministers and governments elsewhere may also guess wrong sometimes.
I say the minister did guess wrong, and we cannot hope to compete with the low cost countries of South America and Australia. The figures show that in 1947 the Argentine supplied 500,000,000 pounds of choice beef to the United Kingdom at half the price paid under our contract. Large quantities of Australian and New Zealand beef are now supplied at almost the same price as the Argentine received. We must do our share to feed the hungry of Great Britain and Europe, but we should not make the farmers suffer in order to do so. We have been doing our share; on a per capita basis we have supplied twice as much as the United States. We shall continue to do so, for we must not allow the support to come from another direction and have these countries turn to communism.
On one market day in Chicago, Great Britain bought more beef on that market at world prices than she normally buys from Canada in seven months. At page 937 of Hansard for February 28 of last year the Minister of Agriculture admitted that he and the government thought the natural market for Canadian cattle was the United States. During the war I was not against the embargo on our cattle going to the United States, because I felt the feeding of our troops, our own people and our allies came first. Now, however, I suggest to him that if we could again ship our cattle to the United States it would have the effect of driving down American prices and enabling Great Britain to purchase cattle there at a much better price. In this way it would not only help our farmers but would also help Great Britain. The minister said we could only ship our high grade cattle to the United States market, but we will have a large canned meat business with Europe for some time to come. I am sure that as President Truman considers meat rationing again, we could arrange very good terms of entry for our meat.
Then I suggest that we investigate the meat industry from the farmer to the consumer, to bring into the open what the producer, the packer and the retailer do and what they receive for their services. I believe it would
open the eyes of consumers to learn just how much more the producer, that is the farmer, does for his money, and that the real spread comes between the retailer and the consumer in the form of a thirty per cent mark-up. Under controls set up by the government the retailer was allowed a mark-up of thirty per cent, which equals at least nine cents per pound on meat sold over the counter. That situation still prevails and will continue to prevail until they get back into competitive business, free from any government control. It is my belief that when government controls were set the spread allowed the retailer was too great, which has worked to the disadvantage of both the farmer and the consumer.
The house knows how much our hog production has dropped. It has gone from five million hogs in 1943 to less than two million today. Many times in the past I warned the house that this would happen unless the price of feed was controlled together with the price of hogs. I asked the house to arrange that western feed grains be made readily available to stock raisers in eastern Canada, so the farmer would not have to make a trip almost every day to get a couple of hundred pounds of feed. We were then trying to capture the British bacon market, and a good supply of feed was essential. The farmer could not maintain his hog production at the price he was receiving. He lost money, and with the margin of profit on all his products cut so fine he could not afford it. Production is down; the cost of living is up.
The complete answer to the problem of the high cost of living is production and more production of food. Only by keeping the markets fully supplied will the people of Canada be able to buy within their means. In order to keep up the production of food there must be a reward in it for the farmer. There is not now the urge that drove him throughout the war. The desire to do his share in the war effort cannot be carried over into peace. Now he rightly feels that he should receive some reward for his unfailing efforts under ceiling prices. It is only fair that he should now receive prices which will give him a good return on his investment of time and labour. He must be freed of all things that hamper his production. He cannot continue to produce when he knows that though the prices of everything he buys are going up, the government is considering putting back the ceiling on all those things he has to sell. Every effort should be made to take from his shoulders anything that. will keep him from producing to the greatest extent possible.
The Address-Mr. Aylesworth

Here I want to say something about the income tax on farmers and market gardeners. I think I can say, with every rural member of this house, that the greatest threat to increased production on the part of the farmers 'is the income tax. They know that if they increase their production and thus increase their income the government will step in and take away from them the surplus their increased efforts have gained for them. Because of this they are cutting down on their stock, and in some cases reducing their herds to less than one-half the usual number. They have seen their neighbours called before income tax officials who questioned their statements as to how much feed they fed their stock, how much their feed cost them, and so on. They have been questioned by men who are very good at figures but who have not the slightest idea how much feed it takes to raise stock. I say to hon. members that, more than anything else, it is the fear of income tax that keeps the farmer from increasing his production, and therefore this is partly the reason for our high cost of living.
To add to the misery of the farmer the Department of National Revenue, income tax division, is now on his trail with a complicated income tax form which is accompanied by an even more complicated booklet of instruction. I would recommend that all hon. members read an article by "I.N.S." in the Ottawa Journal of January 13, 1948, on the new income tax forms and booklets. It tells of an imagined conversation between a farmer and the Minister of National Revenue on the form and the booklet, and is based on questions and answers contained in the booklet. It shows that in order to complete the forms the farmer must keep a daily journal of all his transactions, andi I am sure that to follow all the instructions each farmer would have to hire a clerk to make the preparations for filing the income tax return. I suggest that income tax forms for farmers be as simple as, or even more simple than, any income tax forms. Those who make their living from the soil are as honest as most Canadian men. They could be asked to compute how much they made during the year, how much they figured for the wear and tear on their farm during the year, and then pay their income tax, if any, from basic tables. When one considers that the average farm income for the United States is $779 per year and1 is probably lower in Canada, and a married man's exemption is greater than that, one will see that not many farmers will have to file income tax forms. But just in case they do, they have to keep records until the end of the year. In 1946, out of 652,928 farmers

only 136,039 filed forms, and only 27,411 paid income tax. How much did it cost to prepare these new forms and new booklets? How much will it cost to collect the income tax due from those, who have to pay? Will the department break even?
I should like also to say a few words on behalf of the market gardeners and vegetable growers. These people do not know just where they stand. If they could receive some assurance from the government as to the length of time the foreign exchange conservation measure will be enforced, they could plan their production so that they could keep the home markets supplied. They do not want to go to the expense of buying seeds, paying high labour costs and producing a good supply of vegetables, only to find that next fall, when their produce is ready for market, they will be faced with a market flooded with produce from the United States. As the house well knows, during the past years the market gardeners have not been producing fully because they could not compete with this flood of United States produce. To bring about an increase in the Canadian production of vegetables, let us make sure that Canadians will have the home market.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I strongly urge the government to follow these suggestions which I have offered1:
1.	Give the farmer relief from income tax and simplify his method of payment.
2.	Make available western feed grains in large quantities.
3.	Open the United States market to Canadian cattle.
4.	Increase production to bring down the high cost of living through giving the farmer something worthwhile for which to work.
5.	Cut out the hidden taxes which do so much to increase the cost of living for everybody, and especially for the low income earner.
6.	Promote a better understanding between the consumer and the producer.
In these ways only can we look in the future to a productive and prosperous Canada.

I merely mention this situation to show members of the house the position in which the beef feeder finds himself through having to pay higher prices for his feeder steers before putting them in the feed lot. Unless he can sell for a correspondingly high price at the end of his season's operations he is going to face stark disaster. This is free enterprise, and no one will object to free enterprise as far as it goes. Where the difficulty comes is that the government permits free enterprise to be in full operation when it comes to putting feeder steers into the feed lots, but the government interferes and checks private enterprise and free enterprise at the other end of the line. That is where the difficulty lies. The government has put ceilings on but has neglected to take care of floors in the beef feeding industry.
The result of this whole situation is that in 1947-48 the feeders of steers paid between 13 and 15 cents a pound for their beef steers before putting them into the lots. This year costs of feeding are very high. I asked a question the other day concerning the increased costs of feeding, and the minister gave a flippant answer. It may have been technically accurate, because I do not know the figures he had in mind. He did not give them to us but he certainly gave the house and the country a picture which was far from accurate.
I should like to quote some men who are in position to know because they are right there on the firing line.

Suppose you were one of those beef producers and you had a hundred first-class steers in your feed lot and it was costing you 70 cents a day to feed each of those steers, $70 a day for the lot. After you bought the steers and began to feed them the government entered into the picture and took the controls off oats and barley and practically ruined your chances. The government did nothing to take care of the price
The Address-Mr. Blackmore

of hay. The government neglected practically every one of your costs, allowing 'them to go up at will, and then sat right on the lid and refused utterly to do anything to help you out of the difficulty into which their fallacious policy had forced you. That is the situation faced by these feeders, and here we Canadians are, whose welfare depends on beef, along with the other fine things Canada can produce! We have a responsibility to Britain across the water because of the contract to deliver beef, and yet we are supinely disregarding the factors which make for the production of beef. I sometimes wonder how it is with people in western Europe; if they ever get to know about the foolhardy way in which we do things, how they can resist going in with Russia. I do not know whether Russia does things right, but it is a sure thing that the governments in our country do not do things right.
There is no visible limit to the problem which these feeders face. At the present time there is a fall in prices largely because of the uncertainty induced by the removal of ceilings on beef, and then the implication on the part of government agencies that beef controls will be reimposed. But the government have neglected the whole matter so that no beef producer knows where he stands. About five days ago I asked when the government proposed to announce its policy with respect to the reimposition of controls, and I was promised that the government would consider the matter. Apparently they will consider it until some time in May when these men have been forced completely out of business. It seems to me the government should discharge a lot of the boys they have on the job and see if they cannot employ a few men who know something about their business.
Just to show you that what I am saying is based on facts and realities, may I quote again from George Ross's statement in the Lethbridge Herald of February 20, 1948. He tells of his experience with the packers, and indicates the position they are in-and let no one say glibly, "Well, it is private enterprise that is to blame". It is the government that is to blame. Look at this picture:
He was told-
This is Mr. Ross.
-by representatives of the meat packers that their coolers were full of the higher grades of beef which they had bought at prices too high for the meat board to take them for export.
Which means that the packing houses are filled with beef which cannot be exported to Britain under the present agreement without loss, while the feed lots of the beef

feeders are filled with beef of too high a quality to be sold to Britain. The Canadian public will not buy it because it is too high in price, and the government refuses to let the beef go into the United States where the people there would buy it. If you can imagine a situation more nearly bordering on lunacy than that, you have a vivid imagination.
Now there is another aspect to this whole thing. First there is our responsibility to our own people of tomorrow to make sure that enough beef is produced for them, and second there is our responsibility to the countries of western Europe, Britain among them. Let us have a few figures to show how serious that responsibility is and what we have done in the past.
Our first beef agreement with Britain in recent times was from January 1, 1944, to December 31, 1B45. The price which Britain paid was $22.75 for top grade and $21.75 for next grade, and they agreed to take 100 million pounds. During the term we shipped to them 348,500,000 pounds. Those were the days when we were producing beef as Canada can produce beef. We had1 a great number of our finest beef producers overseas, but we were doing fairly well with the old men and the cripples.
From January 1, 1946, to December 31, 1946, we had another agreement with Britain, this time at $22.75 and $21.75. Britain agreed to take 60.000,000 pounds that year and we shipped them roughly 120 million pounds. We had not entirely ceased to produce beef on a free and buoyant basis, and the people still had some confidence in the government's management of beef. Canadians were eating a bit more, but we were getting home a number of men who could produce beef. There was no sufficient reason why we should not have been able to supply all the demands of our own consumers and still ship as much as we did in 1944-45.
From January 1, 1947, to December 31, 1947, we had another agreement. In this agreement the British agreed to pay $24.25 and $23.25. They agreed to take 120 million pounds, and Canada supplied them roughly 36,500,000 pounds. Canadians were eating more. But let us remember once more that there were home now the strong and vigorous boys who had been overseas, and others were back from the munition factories. So there was no good reason why they should not have been producing beef. Why were they mot? Simply because government policy was not such as to encourage them or give them confidence.

The Address-Mr. Blackmore
I suppose the Minister of Agriculture will get up and give a talk about how we did not have coarse grains, or something of the sort. Perhaps that entered into it, but it is a strange thing that the coarse grain problem began to trouble us after the war I
From January 1, 1948, we have another agreement up to December 31 of this year, in which the British are to take 45,000,000 pounds. Unless we do something to manage wisely our production in Canada we shall fall far short of supplying even that number of million pounds.
When the Minister of Agriculture was travelling through the west he told the farmers constantly that he could not afford to let beef go to the United States because he needed it for Britain. It does not look as though he is much concerned about Britain for the next year.
In a general way, what is the importance of this little area I represent in this house and for which I have the honour to speak here? It is the Lethbridge federal riding. In that federal riding there are situated two sugar factories. There are 100,000 acres of land for which irrigation is supplied so that the farmers can produce a great quantity of hay as well as a great quantity of beets. There is an enormous amount of feed coming out of the beet sugar factories, and a great deal of feed comes as a result of the canning activities that are taking place in three or four canning factories in operation in that area. It is an excellent area for producing beef, one of the choicest in Canada. All around that fine area, where water is available for the land, there are hills on which ranchers raise beef in abundance and where they can raise it in even greater abundance.
Now they have 40.000 beef in the feed lots this year. And 40,000 beef steers are a lot of steers! But this is the kind of thing that is disregarded by the federal government in my area, not to mention other areas in the country.
What is the remedy? I have hesitated to condemn the policy of the Minister of Agriculture, or whoever sets his policy for him, poor man. I had hesitated to condemn that policy because I was not entirely sure that I had at my disposal all the factors that entered into the situation; but today, I am afraid, I must join those who completely condemn him in respect of his policy. We find, from the evidence that I have today adduced, that the British people cannot buy our high class beef, our red' label and blue label brands, because they cannot pay the price which o-ur feeders must have in order to produce this year those
brands of beef. We have found also that the Canadian people seem to be unwilling to buy the beef because it is too high in price for them. If we continue today to refuse to allow our producers of beef to sell their product across the line in the United States it simply means that we shall force into bankruptcy, perhaps permanently, but at least for a period of years, a fine lot of producers of beef, both stock raisers and feeders, who would be in a position to produce at least 40,000 beef a year for many years to come. It means w'e shall force these feeders into bankruptcy, force them out of business, when by just a slight modification of our policy we could avoid all that. W'hat the beef feeders want is that they be permitted to sell their beef across the line.
I do not go so far at the present time as to advocate that the embargo be lifted completely, thus raising the cost of beef to our Canadian consumers or interfering with our commitments to Britain; but I do suggest this as a solution which is worthy of serious consideration. Why not allow the beef feeders to sell their red label beef, as they come to fitness in the feed lots, across the line in the United States, thereby removing the danger of driving the feeder into bankruptcy? Why not, in a frank and straightforward manner, approach the packers and say to them: "Show us your inventories. Show us the amount of beef you have on hand which you cannot afford to sell under the British agreement or to the Canadian consumer at present prices, and we will agree to allow you to send that beef across the line into the United States market?" In this way we can gain a great many dollars and we can remove the pressure on the beef feeders which is now simply unbearable and which if it is allowed to continue will result in complete disaster.

First I wish to express my personal regrets that the former genial Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) is no longer at that post. We all realize that the portfolio of fisheries which he is at present occupying is in all probability only a haven where he is riding out the storm before he goes to that place to which all good old-line politicians want to go. While we all miss him in the Department of Trade and Commerce, may I urge him to make use of
The Address-Mr. Burton

his opportunity in his new department to let the world know that in the cold waters of the northern part of the three prairie provinces we have an abundance of the finest fish. He can help, if he will only do so, to provide a steady and appreciative market for them.
To the new Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe)-who, by the way, is also absent-may I say that in my humble opinion he is much more suited to the other department over which he presides than he is to the Department of Trade and Commerce. Frankly I have always admired that man's ability as a builder. He is a builder, not a trader. We all appreciate the tremendous job he did during the war, and we regret that his organizing ability and driving force are not to be confined solely to the task of reconstruction. Nevertheless I wish him well and urge him to see to it that so long as he presides over the Department of Trade and Commerce a fair amount of wheat shall be exported through the port of Churchill. For this year our minimum objective should be not less than 25,000,000 bushels. Furthermore every effort should be made to establish a shipping route between Churchill and the ports in the maritime provinces. Some day I hope to have the opportunity of taking a day-or a part of a day, I hasten to say before I frighten you, Mr. Speaker-to give you the full story of the Hudson Bay route, and prove to your satisfaction that the proper use of it will be of benefit to all parts of Canada.
The new Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Gregg)-whom I congratulate on being present-has, I am sure, the good wishes of members on all sides of the house. May I urge upon the minister that if we could spend over $25,000 to train a young man for a job of destruction, surely we can give that young man and his comrades in all branches of the armed forces enough on which to live decently while they are preparing themselves for peaceful pursuits. In my opinion the minister should take immediate steps to give further assistance to single as well as married veteran students.
When we were summoned to the other place on December 5 to hear the speech from the throne I had hopes that the government would at last recognize the urgency of the situation and for once give to this country the leadership it so badly needs. But what a hope 1 I should have known from past experience that nothing can be expected from this government except partisan expediency. Just look at the record. Even the little that was done

prior to the Christmas recess must be done all over again because the government refused to listen to the advice from us in this part of the house. Even before the Prime Minister's announcement this afternoon, rumours had been heard that the government was planning to have only a long week-end for the Easter recess. They will realize that this will mean that only the members from Ontario and Quebec will be able to spend Easter at home, whereas the rest of us who come from a great distance will be unable to go home and be back in time.

speechtext:
Let me say this, Mr. Speaker. As far as I am concerned, the Prime Minister is welcome to his anniversary parties and to his Liberal conventions. No doubt his anniversaries come all too frequently, while his Liberal conventions are too few and far between. But he should not make it impossible for members who come from great distances to be with their families at Christmas or Easter, the two days of the year above all when every family man should be at home with his family. I join with the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank) in the hope that all possible pressure will be put upon the Prime Minister and the government to have these points taken into consideration. And at this time may I offer the suggestion that in future we assemble early in November, complete the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne and initiate as much legislation as possible before the holiday season. That would give us a chance to dispose of the budget before the end of the fiscal year, thereby avoiding the necessity of voting interim supply, and in most years we would be able to prorogue by mid-spring. In all seriousness I urge this suggestion upon the government, not merely for due consideration but for favourable consideration.
Had this debate been dealt with in the proper way in all probability I would not

The Address-Mr. Burton
have taken part in it; but since so little has been done on behalf of the people I have the honour to represent I must protest, otherwise the government might come to the conclusion that my people were satisfied. The people of my constituency came from almost every state of the union to the south, from almost every country in continental Europe, from the British isles, and from almost every province in this dominion. We, or our fathers before us, carved our homes out of the wilderness. We have lived there in peace and harmony as good neighbours, and with very few exceptions my people would not want to live anywhere else. To all of us Canada is tops. We all know that at present we are, so to speak, sitting on top of the world. But the majority of the people in my constituency feel that this is because of the efforts of the people of this country, and in spite of the lack of vision on the part of this government. In their opinion this government has failed; therefore I have no hesitation in supporting the want of confidence motion contained in the amendment moved by my leader, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) on December 9, in these words:
Tbat this house regrets that Your Excellency's advisers have failed to use the powers provided by parliament to control prices, and by their actions have caused alarming increases in the cost of living and a dangerous lowering of the living standards of the Canadian people.
The people of my constituency believe that if we could plan for war and destruction, surely we can also plan for peace and construction. I would list their main complaints as follows: first, the government's ill-advised policy of decontrol, which has caused the cost of living of every person to go up, as well as the farmer's cost of production; second, removal of the subsidies on feed grains and other commodities. By the way, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) and the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) failed to accept the invitation I extended to them to come to Humboldt during the Christmas recess and explain the policy of the government in this respect. I did hear that the minister went to Lethbridge, however, to meet the cattle raisers. From the speech of the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) this afternoon I gathered that the minister did not learn very much there, and I suggest that in all probability they should not have had the sign I was told they had at their meeting place: "All stockmen check their guns here before going in."
On behalf of the people I represent I call upon the government, and particularly on these two hon. gentlemen, to quit their play-acting and put all coarse grains marketed in the prairie provinces under the control of the
wheat board, also to come to a settlement with the farmers who delivered their oats and barley in the early part of the present crop year. While as yet I have not had an opportunity of studying the announcement made this afternoon by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, I am satisfied from the little I could hear of it that the plan will be far from satisfactory. Furthermore, regardless of the announcement, having in mind the suggestion made by the Minister of Agriculture on different occasions that the elevator companies should make this adjustment, I say that would be most unfair to both the farmers and the elevator companies concerned. Those who had delivered their feed in regular volume would be penalized, while those who aggravated the shortage of feed by withholding delivery could make good fellows of themselves under this plan. This muddle was caused by the government's ill-advised policy, and the government should clear it up. They have the power, if only they will use it, to deal with those who made undue profits.
We in the C.C.F. group during the past several years have endeavoured to bring home to the Minister of Agriculture the urgent need of a sensible, stable livestock program. Here I should like to quote from a letter I received from one of my constituents, and it is only one of many. He says:
Now the farmers will not raise as many pigs and cattle as they did before. I for one will not raise any more than for my own use, and the big majority of farmers that I meet say the same thing. I know a man that used to raise as much as two hundred hogs, and today he has not one pig on the place. Then there are others that used to have ten and eleven milk cows, and now they have only one or two. So you can see that the Liberals are going to ruin the country if they stay in power much longer.
The third complaint of my constituents is that they do not like the government's excessive taxation policy, especially the unconstitutional imposition of the excise tax; nor do they approve of the "turnip nibbling" austerity program of the Minister of Finance.
Their fourth complaint is that they do not like the new income tax forms. For several years we were promised a sensible simplified form for farmers. Look at what we get now. When I first saw that form from a distance and noticed the dark edge I thought it was black. It reminded me of when I was a youngster, when operations for appendicitis were just beginning to be performed. They were something to be dreaded, and we saw many obituary notices which read something like this: "John Doe was stricken with appendicitis. The operation was successful but the patient died." In that connection I should like to quote from another letter I received
The Address-Mr. Burton

from one of my constituents, where he said, 'I'll bet the man who drafted these forms never made his living on a farm". I could quote from a number of other letters, but I am afraid the language used in most of them would be unparliamentary.
Then, fifth, the people of my constituency do not like this government's immigration policy. What burns them up most is that in spite of official and semi-official announcements which pretend to give priority to people's relatives, the relatives of good citizens of this country wanting to come to Canada, the officials of this department seem to be able to find ways and means of preventing them from coming here. They are preventing these people wdio have made good in the past from helping their destitute relatives in the old countries, who wish to come here to start life anew.
This is the first day of March. We have made very little progress since the speecn from the throne was read on December 5. Any one of the legislatures of the three prairie provinces would have done twice as much in half the time. The Saskatchewan house opened on February 5. They had debated and disposed of the speech from the throne by February 20, besides advancing a great deal of other business in preparation for committee work. You will realize of course, Mr. Speaker, that most of its members are farmers and, as you know, we farmers pride ourselves on cutting a straight furrow. And in addition to that, once having put our hands to the plow, we know from experience that the only way to finish a field is to stick to the job and to do it in a systematic fashion.
I still recall the ridicule of our opponents when they asked the people to stop and to think before allowing a group of farmers, preachers and teachers to carry on their business for them in Regina. Well, I still have circulars in my files from the bond dealers quoting prices of 80 to 85 cents on the dollar, and in some cases even less than that, for Saskatchewan government bonds in 1943. Those same bonds are now changing hands from time to time at prices from twelve to fifteen cents above par.
One of the first measures to be put on the statute books by the present provincial government in Saskatchewan was an act to give security to the farmers on their farms. We of the C.C.F. have constantly adhered to the policy we adopted in the very beginning of our organization, namely that if the family farm is to survive, then the farmer must have security of tenure on that farm. But as property rights come under provincial juris-
diction the details of the method of doing that were of necessity left to the respective provinces.
Prior to the organization of the C.C.F. in the early thirties over 12,000,000 acres of the best land in Saskatchewan were under the control of the mortgage companies. In many instances a farmer was only a tenant on land which used to belong to him; he was a tenant under the most vicious form of absentee ownership. Farmers in their own conventions decided to advocate a system of use-lease titles whereby the provincial government only at the request of the farmer was to Obtain an adjustment on the debt, pay off the balance of the mortgage and then obtain title. In turn it would issue a use-lease to the farmer and his heirs.
The farmer-labour group in their first provincial gathering adopted that idea. Later, at our first convention, this was changed to a use-hold title which would have given the holder all the rights and privileges of a Torrens title, except the right to mortgage. This became the most controversial issue of the provincial election of 1934; and our opponents were successful in leading the majority of farmers to love their mortgages to such an extent that they hated to give them up. At our next annual convention, attended by delegates from all parts of the province, we reaffirmed our belief in the fundamental principle of security of tenure to the farmer on his own farm, but decided by an almost unanimous vote to change the details as to how that was to be done. Then a policy was worked out with respect to a crop failure clause to be incorporated in all mortgages and agreements of sale of farm lands.
As I said before, the placing of this provision on the statute books of the province was one of the first acts of the present provincial administration. But owing to the fact that some of these clauses have been challenged, I shall say nothing further about the matter except this: that if unfortunately we are preve'nted from giving protection in this manner, we shall not rest. Rather we shall continue our efforts to provide that security to the farmers, when they are faced with crop failures and low prices, both of which are beyond their control.
Let me repeat that we shall also continue to adhere to the fundamental principle of the farmer having security on his own farm. This brings me to a question which is often asked, and is even asked in this house on occasions. In the majority of cases I believe the question is asked honestly, although in others I have

The Address-Mr. Burton
my suspicions as to the motives behind the asking of it. The question, regardless of the motive, is this: Why does the C.C.F. advocate socialization of other people's property, but not that of our own farms? The answer to the question is this: that we do not advocate the socialization of any property, be it a farm .or otherwise, unless it comes within the category of a monopoly, or otherwise gives to an individual or to a small group of individuals, the opportunity to dominate and exploit their fellow men. There are of course other measures which provide for expropriation for the common good. The ownership of a farm by the individual farmer does not give that power of domination and exploitation; but when our grains and livestock enter the channels of domestic and export markets they are very often then manipulated in a fashion contrary to the well-being of the community at large. For that reason we support the co-operatives on the one hand and government agencies such as the wheat board on the other, and are constantly urging the extension of these and other socially owned undertakings.
Our government in Saskatchewan has made a good start along these lines. In a number of instances they are operating industries about which the so-called1 free enterprisers never concerned themselves. In addition they have set up a department of co-operatives to assist in the development of co-operative enterprises. They have given special aid to the organization and operation of a horse meat packing plant, a flax crushing plant, and have given special consideration to a group of veterans who have begun operations on a co-operative farm.
In addition, they have set up sixteen crown corporations which are engaged in the industrial development of the province. These consist of a woollen mill, a shoe factory, a modern tannery, a brick plant and other clay mining for the production of pottery; a sodium sulphate plant, a timber marketing board and a box factory; a fish marketing board and filleting plants; a fur marketing service, and a bus service which is being extended to all parts of the province as rapidly as new vehicles can be obtained. I may say that arrangements have been made so that long distance interprovincial bus services can be carried on by the firms that have given good service in the past.
The government established an air service for the northern areas and have three other planes that are used in the air ambulance service whereby emergency cases are taken to hospital for a nominal fee of $25. This has
proven to be of great value in areas far from other means of transportation. The power commission which the previous administration always operated in the red has expanded its services, reduced the rates three times and for the past two years or more has returned a substantial net surplus. The government telephone system, while showing a surplus under the previous administration, also extended its services and increased its net surplus.
The government insurance office has done better than the most optimistic of our supporters ever expected. In connection with automobile accident insurance the car owner as well as the pedestrian has protection that cannot be equalled elsewhere, at a fee which is much less than the ordinary protection cost. The government is co-operating with private interests in the exploration and development of our oil, gas and salt resources. While a number of the government-operated ventures are still in their trial period, and others are handicapped by being unable to secure sufficient equipment, the fact is that during the last fiscal year they brought in a net return of over $2,250,000. For the first nine months of the present fiscal year they boosted the net returns to over $2,600,000. In the meantime more private corporations and companies were registered than in any previous year.
Great progress has been made in extending social services, of which the provincial-wide hospitalization plan tops the list. The next is the free medical service provided for all old age pensioners, blind pensioners and those on mother's allowance, et cetera. Free cancer treatment is provided, and the province has assumed full responsibility for the care and treatment of the mentally ill. Tuberculosis patients were previously taken care of by the anti-tuberculosis league. The government has increased the assistance given to this noble work.
In the educational field the government has increased grants, provided free textbooks and to a greater extent than ever before is endeavouring to provide equal educational opportunity and the spreading of costs. The larger unit of administration act was placed on the statute books by the previous administration, but it was done in such a way that not even its most ardent supporters felt safe in making use of it. The present government amended the act and now over two-thirds of the schools of the province are operated under the larger units of administration. Aid to agriculture has been increased and the highlights of this are the establishment of feed
The Address-Mr. Burton

banks, the extension of services rendered by agricultural representatives, and the encouragement of veterinary services for livestock.
During the first two years most of the highway department's appropriation had to be spent on the maintaining and reconstruction of highways which had been allowed to deteriorate under the previous administration. During the past two years they have embarked on the largest program of up-to-date highway construction ever undertaken in the province out of current revenue.
I should like to impress upon the federal government the urgency and necessity of undertaking the construction of an all-weather paved highway from coast to coast. This not only would be an asset to the nation but in my opinion could properly be listed as a defence project. Had the governments of the past in times of wide unemployment undertaken the construction of a paved Trans-Canada highway, besides giving useful employment we would have had the use of the highway throughout those years. The need for the highway is there. Even when it is possible to motor under the best of circumstances in certain times of the year we still cannot go to the western provinces by an all-Canada route. This is something that we should have. The highway could be constructed so cheaply in the three prairie provinces you could well afford to have both a north and south branch.
In addition the federal government could give assistance in the construction of allweather highways running north and south in the province. We hear a great deal from time to time about the desirability of providing accommodation for United States tourists. I think it is also the responsibility of the federal government to assist provincial governments in building some of these main arterial highways.
Although our government in Saskatchewan is supported mainly by farmers it has placed on the statute books some of the best labour legislation in existence. In addition our government practises what it preaches by encouraging the members of its civil service to bargain with them collectively through their union.
I appreciate having had the opportunity this afternoon to lay before the government some of the problems that confront the people of my constituency. I appreciate also having had the opportunity of placing before the house details of what ordinary common folk, farmers, preachers and teachers, have done about things which come under their jurisdiction in the government of Saskatchewan.
I ask every hon. member to realize that if we are to get through this period of recon-

struction without undue hardship it is up to all of us to bend our efforts to such an extent that never again shall we have in this country exploitation by monopoly and at the same time poverty facing our people.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the debate on the address ill reply to the speech from the throne the choice of subject is left wide open, and during this debate hon. members who have taken part therein have covered a great range of subjects. I propose to discuss some factors of human relationships in our national economy and to warn against the growth of communism in Canada. I intend to be explicit in certain things so that no one will have room to twist my words and give a wrong interpretation of my attitude toward any sector of the population.
I am a firm believer in trade unions and the -right of collective bargaining, which communism destroys. I believe that through organization the position of labour has vastly improved in recent years. I believe in giving to every person a fair, but not an unfair, opportunity of improving his or her position through personal initiative. I recognize that public utilities constitute a field for government or municipal ownership, and that other public services are adaptable to -co-operative ownership and operation. Otherwise I support private enterprise with safeguards against practices that unduly increase prices to the consumer. With this limitation I believe that Canadian business and industry should be organized, financed, developed and managed by Canadians, individually or in groups.
Agriculture is our No. 1 basic industiy, and I regard profitable farming as an indispensable requirement for full employment in our urban centres and for industrial prosperity. I favour generous assistance, as -I am sure all hon. members do, to veterans and their dependents and to all who, through incapacity or age, cannot earn for themselves. One additional assistance is imperative in my opinion, namely, provision for medical and hospital treatment.
I oppose government control by special interest groups. I believe parliament should be representative of all vocations. Our population divides itself largely into two main groups: one, those who -work close to nature in developing and preparing resources of the farm, the forest, the sea and the mines from which come food, clothing and shelter for all; two, those who work these products further through stages of processing and distribution by means of labour, professional and clerical services, education, science, invention and manufacture. It is

The Address-Mr. Gladstone
largely between the first and last of this second group, labour and manufacturing, that our antagonism, arises, and where sometimes inequality of opportunity exists under the terms of the laws set down by parliament. I wish to deal with these two groups, industry and labour, associating therewith considerations of the theoretical versus the practical in our national economy.
First of all, I will consider industry. In my opinion it is grossly unfair to stigmatize industrialists as profiteers because some may have taken advantage of circumstances to amass fortunes. We ought to strengthen our legislation against the greedy and unscrupulous. Studies should be made to further preventive measures such as may be possible through dominion-provincial co-operation to deal with combines, mergers and the regulation of powers granted under the Companies Act.
The burden of debt places a limit on the undertakings of governments and municipalities. Home owners are ambitious to see their homes free of debt. War added enormously to the debt of Canada. Like home owners, our government should strive to reduce debt to some extent each year, especially during prosperous years. The main source of funds for the reduction of debt must come from profits earned. If we destroy the opportunity of business to earn profits where will be the opportunity to reduce our debt? It is imperative that industry should contribute generously toward the reduction of our national debt after providing a reasonable return on the money invested1. But, first of all, in any industry there should be ample provision for plant modernization and for reserves of working capital whereby industry can carry on through any period of recession, in the interests of highest employment and a minimum lay-off of employees.
Changes in industry through research and invention may see one product replaced by a new product in a very short time. These and other hazards are a constant menace to the continued production of many lines. Speaking of hazards, let us take as an example the former silk manufacturer. He finds today that his product has been replaced largely through plastics, nylons, mercerized cottons and so forth. The same is true of aluminum. This product is finding new competition in magnesium, which is twenty-five per cent lighter and seventy-five per cent stronger than steel. The iceman no longer cuts ice on the rivers and lakes since refrigeration was developed. Take the hazards that the telephone
and telegraph companies have in sleet storms which are so common in this country, requiring the expenditure of tens of thousands of dollars to replace poles and wires.
No industry can survive without machinery as modern as that of its competitors either at home or abroad. Costly laboratories are a necessity of the major industries. New products are developed through research by skilled engineers and scientists. Provision for the continuance of an industry is a justifiable charge against profits earned, and it is vital to continued employment. Expenditures for research would not be available either in time or in amount if approval rested with the government at Ottawa. Disregarding costs, in wartime great organizations of experts can be employed by a government, but not in peacetime.
Let me turn, Mr. Speaker, to some of the considerations that are involved in the successful operation of industries. Mention has been made of some steps taken toward the socialization of industry by the C.C.F. government of Saskatchewan. I would remind you that this experiment commenced during a period of prosperity when goods were in short supply. There is nothing creative in taking over an established industry. I am told that the losses of some industries are pooled with the profits of others so that all may be kept going. Management in industry has to reckon with possible losses as well as with profits. The thing that matters is the progressive development of the industry and its continuance during bad years as well as during good years.
It will be realized that I am a supporter of the right of every person to improve his or her opportunities through the exercise of initiative and by hard work. Let me give an example of the benefaction that came from the inventiveness of one man. That man worked at an idea after his day's work was done and he developed an engine of simple design that could be made cheaply. That man was Henry Ford. The Ford may have been a Tin Lizzie, but it brought the pleasures and health stimulation of nature's farms, forests and lakes to millions of city dwellers.
Henry Ford had a heart for his employees. Nearly thirty years ago, when wages were low, he established a minimum of $5 a day for even the humble sweepers in his plant. The Henry Ford attitude toward employees prevails in many industries today and should be encouraged.
The London chamber of commerce had a survey made of some nine industries in the
The Address-Mr. Gladstone

city of London where the manufacture is carried on of such goods as plumbers' and steamfitters' supplies, threshing machines, hosiery, refrigerators, concrete machinery, doors, cranes, shoes, radios and home appliances. The survey showed total sales of $16,921,375 for those nine industries. Total costs of everything, except wages, salaries and taxes, including materials, outside services, light and power, freight, printing, advertising, insurance, interest and depreciation amounted to $9,529,055. Taxes, including sales tax, amounted to $1,951,052. The remainder was divided as follows: paid 'to workers, $4,612,834; paid to shareholders, $292,166; the remainder being reinvested in buildings, machinery, and working capital in the amount of $536,268. The division of the sales dollar was 56J cents for materials; 11J cents for taxes; 271 cents for workers; \\ cents to the shareholders; 31 cents for new buildings, machinery, inventory, working capital and reserves.
Out of the $5,441,268 that remained after deduction of total cost of materials, et cetera, the workers received 85 per cent, and the shareholders, 15 per cent.
One cannot over-emphasize the importance of an industry being strong to provide good working conditions, latest machinery for economic production, and to meet competition, and with ample financing to give freedom of development. This is all in the interests of employment and a high standard of living.
I will turn now from the management side of industry to the part of labour in processing the natural resources. I think it may be well to divide the consideration of the labour element into two parts relating to the past and the future.
Too much credit cannot be given the great masses of the people for their faithful contribution to the war effort, both on the farm and in 'the factory and elsewhere. The government set an example to the world in the methods they employed in keeping our economy well balanced. Some regulations hurt in places; but, all in all, our people responded cheerfully and made sacrifices where necessary to assist in winning the war.
When the war ended we set our sights toward the restoration of what might be regarded as a new normal. Calculations had been much upset through conditions in Europe and' elsewhere which were beyond our control. The import and export trade has not been as anticipated, and we have experienced difficulty in finding dollars to meet our payments to the United States. The United Kingdom is no longer in a position to make payments to us which will offset our requirements for United States dollars.

Labour has been able to retain and increase the scale of wages paid during the war, but these higher wages have been offset by rising prices of most of the necessities of life. The downward trend of commodity prices in the United States gives hope that the peak in prices may have been reached. There is a great backlog of construction need in Canada which we hope can and will be called upon for continued employment at our present higher scale of wages for the maintenance of our high standard of living in Canada.
The situation has compelled the government to take emergency measures to eliminate our purchases from the United States. We dislike these reductions pertaining to fruits and vegetables which are a more considerable item requiring United, States dollars than we may have realized. For instance, according to the Montreal Standard, in normal times sixty-five carloads of oranges and twenty-five carloads of grapefruit come into Montreal every week. Since November last when quotas were established that quantity has been cut in half.
We become ashamed of our complaining when we recall that for six years or more the people of Britain seldom saw an orange or a grapefruit. Advantage of scarcity was being taken in some places and so control prices of citrus fruits have been re-established. Inflated prices were being asked for cabbage, celery and the like, and measures were taken to correct this. The protest of the housewives was justified and timely.
I do not know whether or not it will be regarded as good politics, but I do not hesitate, to give credit to members of parliament in the C.C.F. group for their efforts in parliament in many circumstances for the maintenance of our high standard of living, a sentence which should not be quoted apart from some things I might mention contra. Solvency of Canada must be maintained. I do think they advocate expenditure of money with little consideration as to where the money will come from.	The C.C.F., in
advocating government ownership, point to hydro and to various public utilities as examples of success in public ownership. In Guelph we own and operate our gas and waterworks, transportation system and hydro electric power and1 light distribution most satisfactorily through commissions named annually by the city of Guelph. The control is not in Ottawa; it lies with the electors who pay. Possibly there may be other spheres of public service to which public ownership might well be extended. As a Liberal I can

The Address-Mr. Gladstone
support and promote co-operation in localities where it would seem that the public interest will be served better than through private ownership. But always I would keep the control and direction near to the people %vho pay.
The C.C.F. would nationalize the banks. I disapprove. The people of Canada own the Bank of Canada and thereby exercise certain controls over the privately owned banks. There is no doubt our banks are well managed. It would be disastrous to place discretion as to size of loans in the hands of some government official.
Criticism of industry in Canada comes largely from the C.C.F. party. They give examples of excess profits in some industries and imply that the same may be true in industry generally. I again give members of that group credit for their earnestness and for their contribution toward improvement of social conditions in Canada. They have done well relatively to the things within their own experience, but in relation to industry I fear they frequently expound theories rather than observe practical considerations. The group, having regard to its becoming any considerable factor in government, has a doubtful future. It came into being in Saskatchewan largely through drought conditions and crop failure. Their membership today is generally from Saskatchewan, a few from British Columbia and Manitoba, with but one member in all of Canada east of the great lakes. It cannot be said that experience gives them practical knowledge of the operation of many of the component factors of our economy.
I should like to refer briefly to the picture of the situation in Europe commencing with the early part of this century. We had a prosperous Britain, highly industrialized, and the focal point for the distribution of goods from all corners of the world. We had a Germany that was strong and prosperous through science and invention; but the ambition of the Kaiser for world domination brought on the war of 1914, so disastrous in many respects to the allies and throwing upon Germany a burden of debt against which she struggled for many years. The result was that in desperation a radical party obtained control and, under the dictatorship of Hitler, a new effort through arms came about in 1939, We see the picture of distress today in Europe whereby our empire is in such desperate straits financial and, where the industries of Germany are destroyed and the country dismembered. There came a change in the political alignments in that country and the forcing upon small nations of ideologies that 5849-111
are not a part of democracy. There is surely a lesson there for us in the trend that things may take, where we may be led unwittingly and unsuspectingly from stage to stage into changes in our system of government. I think it is exceedingly desirable that we in Canada, through this period of prosperity, exercise every care and see to it that influences do not undermine the loyalty of many of our people to our democratic form of life. This will come about only through hard times, and I say respectfully to my C.C.F. friends that their chief hope of success in the future may be the result of bard times.
The high cost of living is a matter of concern for all of us in Canada today and means must be found to stop soaring prices and even to roll back prices to some extent. Sir Stafford Cripps, the socialist chancellor of the exchequer in the United Kingdom, has stated that prices cannot be controlled without wages being also controlled. Our hope in Canada is that present scales of wages may be continued while prices in certain places are reduced moderately. There has been demand for rolling back prices to the 1946 level. I would warn that farmers cannot be expected to produce butter at forty-four cents a pound. The ceiling of seventy-three cents may be too high, but it stands there as a barrier against prices soaring to ninety cents and $1 a pound, as in the United States.
Mr. Speaker, our friends in the C.C.F. party-and I am on most friendly terms with all of them-are at the crossroads of their existence as a group of any dimensions in parliament. If conditions deteriorate they may make some gains, but if times are good they are pretty much through. They are good members, so good that if their contribution has pretty much ended, as now constituted, I hope the electors may deal kindly with them by returning many of them to continue their crusading within the ranks of two-party government.
The danger time for Canada is before us. Labour organizers see more difficult times ahead for their unions. If the peak in wage scales has been reached the monthly dues from workers are bound to fall off. The organizers have recognized this danger and hope to meet it by swinging labour into politics as supporters of the C.C.F. This will not succeed, for the reason that very many workers own their own homes. My factory people in Wellington county are solid and sound in their thinking. They fear the extreme in any such movement. The other day I read of a worker who developed a great interest in the socialist party. It went well

speechtext: Order. I must call the attention of the hon. member to the fact that the Speaker should not be questioned from the floor of the house.

speechtext:
Then I withdraw that
question and just ask that you give it your careful consideration. On different occasions I have endeavoured to speak in this house on matters concerning my province. When the Prime Minister had to search for cabinet ministers, thinking he did not have cabinet material in his own ranks; when he had to go abroad with coalition ideas, since Prince Edward Island was not represented in the cabinet I do think he might have extended to members from that province the opportunity to become part and parcel of the government by being included ini the cabinet. However, they do not recognize our province. It always seems to me that there is either discrimination or forgetfulness; and the rights we had prior to 1873 are gradually being taken away from us.
Let me cite one instance. We always had a savings bank in our province. Then this was swallowed up by the Bank of Canada

The Address-Mr. McLure
and we had a branch of that bank in Charlottetown. We were pleased with that until, in the fall of 1947, our branch bank mysteriously disappeared. It was taken, as it were, by thieves in the night, and was gone from us. That branch was something which should have been retained for us.
. It will be clear that this came as a surprise to the people of the province when I say that there was not one manager of a chartered bank, of the five great chartered banks in Charlottetown, who knew anything about the taking away or transfer of the branch of the Bank of Canada from that city.
We made representations to have it remain. Those representations were made to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott). At that time, however, very few ministers were in Ottawa; I believe the Minister of Finance was somewhere in Europe-probably in gay Paree-and we did not get any satisfaction whatsoever. That branch of the Bank of Canada was taken from us. 'Under present circumstances, all the business which our chartered banks have to do with the Bank of Canada must be done through Saint John and Halifax. This procedure is not always in the best interests of banking or bankers in Prince Edward Island.
Similar treatment was meted out to us in connection with our postal service. Again Prince Edward Island has been ignored as a province, and in connection with this work we have been attached to one of the other provinces. I mention these matters because, if there is one thing near and dear to us in Prince Edward Island, certainly it is our rights as a province of the dominion. We were the cradle of confederation, and we resent these practices, small as they may seem to other provinces. We have our rights and we intend to try to hold them, no matter what odds we may come up against.
Having made these few observations respecting discrimination, let me say that we are now dealing with the speech from the throne. I was not in the house when it was read, but after having read it I have come to the conclusion that it was written in a great hurry for that short session. The purpose of the calling of the short session no one has yet been able to understand; unless it was, of course, that the house might be in session during the birthday festivities of the Prime Minister.
We of the maritime provinces, and particularly those of us from Prince Edward Island, had anticipated that the speech from the throne would contain something new and constructive for the maritime provinces. In 5849-111|
order that we might be maintained in our proper sphere we had entertained the hope that some real suggestions on our behalf would be set forth in the speech from the throne. However, it contains nothing more than phraseology which does not mean very much, and certainly does not mean anything to the marrtimes.
For a few moments I shall deal particularly with Prince Edward Island. My province is what might be described as an agricultural province, statistics showing that about sixty-five per cent of the people depend upon farming of different kinds. Next to agriculture come the fisheries. AVe have very few manufacturing plants. As I have said, farming is the great basic industry of our province, and we are proud of the agricultural activities in it, and of its productive soil. We are proud, too, of our industrious and productive farmers who operate the farms in our province. I say without fear of successful contradiction that they have no equal as farmers in any of the other provinces of this whole dominion.
As a province the enterprise of which is almost entirely agricultural, and as one with still greater possibilities ahead, we must look for certain things. We are able to provide the best of foodstuffs for exports, in addition to supplying all the requirements for our own population. Our butter, cheese, potatoes and furs, as well as sundry other products stand ace-high on the markets of the world. As an agricultural province, we must look for assistance along agricultural lines. To be most effective, we must have the best possible forms of transportation. Our transportation facilities must be up to date. We must have better facilities for the cold storage of farm products. We must have better connection with the mainland. Further, let me repeat that we must have proper freight rates for the shipments we have to make.
Speaking of farmers and the agricultural work being done throughout Canada, and particularly in the maritime provinces, I would remind hon. members of what was said by a great biblical writer who, upon looking at the production of food and those who produced it, made this memorable comment:
Moreover the profit of the earth is for all. The king himself is served by the field.
As agricultural members, we must always look to those things which will favour agricultural interests in our provinces. As I said a minute ago, we in Prince Edward Island are producers of foodstuffs, and have always made the complaint that we have not had proper transportation facilities. To a certain extent this condition has been remedied. Since
The Address-Mr. McLure

1912 transportation has greatly improved; yet a great deal more could be done in the interest of the farmers of that province.
As I said, we must have lower freight rates, particularly in connection with the connecting links between the province and the mainland. We have been promised by the different parties that the charges on our ferries would be based upon what it would cost to carry the freight the same distance over a highway. These promises have been partly implemented in connection with certain agricultural products, but if they were fully implemented it would mean that we could transport our surplus foodstuffs to the other maritime provinces where we could find a real market.
If the bridging of the strait of Canso is completed, as surely it must be at an early day, what a market for foodstuffs would be opened up. Our farmers could transport the products of their farms by motor truck direct to Cape Breton island, and on the return trip they could bring back coal, lime or other commodities. Today we have part of that market, but it is under adverse conditions. I understand that the miners, workers and labourers in the great industries on Cape Breton island receive over 830,000,000 in wages annually. This new bridge would certainly provide a new market for a large number of our agricultural products.
There is another matter in connection with my province "which I should like to mention. When victory for the allied forces was in sight a great program of demobilization, reconstruction, et cetera, was announced. The maritime provinces were asked to place their problems before the federal government and Prince Edward Island set up a reconstruction committee as suggested by the federal government. I do not know what treatment was given to New Brunswick and Nova Scotia; but, if it was any shabbier than that given to Prince Edward Island, then I pity those provinces. We have not received anything under that extensive program which was talked about and advertised for years previous.
During the war years of 1939 to 1945 the maritime provinces were neglected. They did not share in the great increase in manufacturing for war purposes. In the case of Prince Edward Island it was practically nil. During those years the government poured out $790 million of the taxpayers' money to build or construct new factories and to expand or rebuild old ones. I do not object to that expenditure because it was for war purposes, but I do object to the way in which it was spent. It should have been divided among

the provinces so that they could all have had a share in manufacturing certain types of goods.
The maritime provinces represented one-tenth of the population of Canada, and yet New Brunswick and Nova Scotia received less than three per cent of this expenditure. Surely they were entitled to at least ten per cent. But Prince Edward Island did not receive even three per cent; we received one one-thousandth of one per cent or the fancy, tiny sum of $1,277. This was to complete a small expansion of a factory which was manufacturing some war materials.

After Recess
