subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Just before the house took recess I was speaking of the large expenditures during wartime and the injustice done to the maritime provinces with respect to these expenditures. For instance, I mentioned that $790 million had been spent to rebuild factories and to construct new ones for war purposes. I said I took no objection to that because it was for war; but let us look for a moment at what happened. According to statistics tabled in this house with reference to the contracts which had been awarded to these firms which had been set up in business, and some created as crown companies, and so forth, the total expenditure was almost $12 billion from 1939 to 1945, or, to be exact, $11,979,200,000. As I said, I am not objecting to these enormous expenditures; they were for war purposes. The objection I take is this, and I think I take it on good grounds. I contend that there should have been a fair distribution of this amount in the maritime provinces. Out of this immense sum of nearly $12 billion, my province received an expense account for the repairs of two or three corvettes and a minesweeper, a paltry sum indeed when compared with the $12 billion that was spent. It is not much wonder that in the maritimes today we have unemployment. I say this to labour and to the labour department, do not take away our labour from the maritime provinces. Do justice to the maritime provinces by building the constructive works which have been promised to us, such as the Canso bridge, the Ohignecto canal on the mainland and so forth. In Prince Edward Island we were promised improved highways and the construction of a highway from Borden to Charlottetown. We were promised a

The Address-Mr. McLure
marine slip and the Brighton bridge. These things were all promised and were held out to the people in the last election on December 11 of last year. Both parties are committed to them.
I wish to speak for a moment with reference to one of these projects that should be built. In my province an essential work could be built which would give employment to from 150 to 200 people annually. I refer to the building of the marine railway slip. When we started to get the ferry system in 1913 that was part of the program. It was included to such an extent that the. government of that day purchased a property on Southport road across from Charlottetown for the building of a drydock. The war of 1914 put an end to the project for the time being. The property is still there. I might say that today they are recommending the building of the marine railway slip at Charlottetown harbour to take care of the repair work of our own steamers and our own ferry boats, and also the different boats that are in the marine service, such as barges and tugboats. All this work has to leave the province annually. It goes to Pictou, Halifax, Saint John and Quebec, and our own people are left unemployed. If this marine slip were built at Charlottetown-and it has been definitely promised to us-we would have employment, the year round for some 150 to 200 men, in the summertime our big ferry ships could be repaired there or have their annual overhaul there, and the other marine boats, tugs, and so forth could be repaired there when they are laid up in the wintertime. If these things were done and if Prince Edward Island were to receive assistance in comparison with what the other provinces are receiving we would have better times in the maritime provinces and no unemployment. Our men would not have to be taken away from those provinces to other places to seek work.
Because these repairs all go to Pictou, Halifax, Saint John and Quebec, our ships are delayed in getting there. Most of these places have so much work on hand that the delay is continued and we are months without our ships back in the regular service. Charlottetown has an excellent harbour; and if we had this marine railway slip I am sure that the steamers making it a port of call, bringing in and taking away freight, would not have to leave for a slight overhaul. The overhaul could take place right in Charlottetown while they are unloading and loading.
I should now like to refer to the building of the Brighton bridge. As I said, these things
were promised by -both parties during the last election, and they were pretty well threshed out not only here but down there during the election.
Another matter to which I wish to refer for a few moments is the tourist trade. As we have all said and keep repeating, Canada has wonderful possibilities in the tourist trade. It is a grand thing to see the provinces interested in that trade. Like the maritimes generally, my province is a real vacation spot. There, where much of the dominion's history originated you will find a tourist's paradise. No place offers more to the real tourist than the Island. There you will find a real climate, not too hot. Even if it is a hot day the gentle sea breezes will temper it nicely to the tourist. There you can see the most beautiful farms and farm scenery, scenery which will bring pleasure to any tourist who travels around.
A few years ago, in co-operation with the provincial government, the Dominion of Canada gave us a national park beginning at Tracadie, or, as we say, Dalvay by the sea. That took in the coastline of Dalvay, Tracadie, Brackley Point, Stanhope, Rustico (not Russia) and Cavendish out to Stanley bridge.
The minister himself said that this national park was an ideal spot. In connection with it we have what is known as the Green Gables golf course. Those who play golf can find no finer golf course than Green Gables, in the land made famous by Canada's greatest writer, the late Lucy Maud Montgomeiy MacDonald. On the sandy beaches of this beautiful national park you will find the best bathing grounds that are to be found anywhere. I might say, however, that the worst feature since we received this park is in the highways that we have by which to reach the park; and I hope that the government, in conjunction with the provincial government, will see to it this year that we have proper approaches leading to our park.
It would take only ten miles to reach the beautiful playgrounds and vacation grounds of Brackley, Stanhope and Dalvay. Then, from Rustico it would take only seven miles, and from New Glasgow a distance of six miles. I am glad to learn that the Department of Mines and- Resources is considering building one of these highways this year. The other day I asked the minister a question regarding which there was a little misunderstanding, a typographical error having occurred. My question had reference to the road from Rustico to Cavendish, to the national park, and I wanted to know when it would be built. I had understood it was to be built on a sixty-forty basis between the two governments. If we had
The Address-Mr. McLure

these roads constructed as they should be, leading to our national park, it would do a great deal for the tourist industry of our province.
There is one thing you can be assured of, Mr. Speaker, and that is that the people engaged in the tourist business in Prince Edward Island are making a real industry out of it. They are endeavouring, to the best of their ability, to cater to the people who come to our shores; and we hope that in years to come, with the assistance of the federal government in the way of good roads, our tourist trade will be materially advanced so that we may have this wonderful vacation spot thronged with visitors during the summer months.
Another matter on which I wish to speak for a few minutes is in reference to social security. You, Mr. Speaker, as well as the members of this house have listened to many excellent appeals on behalf of the aged, the blind, and the veterans of both wars. You have heard about the rehabilitation of these men and you have heard proposals for giving them security in their old age.
I often think there is one class of people who have been greatly neglected, more so in our province than in any other, and for a few minutes I wish to discuss the low-wage bracket earner of the Canadian National Railways when he is put on retirement. There are in my constituency a number of these men who were retired a few years ago and some who have been recently retired, and the amount of their retirement is $25 to $27 a month. That retirement allowance might have been good enough a few years ago; but today it is not sufficient, and I for one would like to see these faithful employees of the Canadian National Railways, retired some years ago, and especially the men receiving less than $150 and down to the lowest, brought up to where they can have a decent living allowance for the rest of their days. Those in the higher brackets who have had higher salaries need not be taken into consideration to the same extent as those in the lower brackets.
There is another class of people to whom I would refer. We have given aid to the blind and the aged; we have provided children's allowances and so on; but in every constituency across Canada we find today people who are crippled, some crippled by severe accidents when they were young, some as they have grown a little older, and some crippled and handicapped from birth. There seems to be no social security for any of these, and I know that in my own constituency there are several of them.
[Hr. McLure.J
I have taken this matter up with the minister of health and welfare, but the answer always comes back that it is a provincial matter. When you go to the provincial house there is always a dispute between city and country, with the consequence that very few of those people are securing anything to help them with the great handicap they have. I hope this government will consider the matter to see that these people have some compensation for themselves.
Another matter I wish to touch upon, and one that is of importance to us, is the question of freight rates.

speechtext:
I wish to say a few words with reference to freight rates. One of the great problems in Canada today is that of freight rates. It touches everybody in every part of the country. Here we are faced in Canada with a government-owned railway system, the Canadian National Railways, one of the greatest railway systems, if not the greatest, in the whole world. This company, after due consideration regarding its expenses and operating income, has applied to the government for a 30 per cent increase in freight rates.
We all know that conditions have changed and that greater demands are being made in every direction, and I may say that if the railways are expected to give the service which is demanded of them, both by the government and by the people of Canada, and if at the same time the demand is made that they pay their own way and make a surplus instead of a deficit, then the task is an impossible one for them.
If the government demand of the railways that they give perfect satisfaction they must also say to the railways, "If you have a deficit we will take care of it," if they are not going to allow them to increase their rates.
In connection with freights, I believe that in the very near future the railway systems of Canada will make a study of what is termed stamp freight rates. What I mean is this. If a man in Halifax writes a letter to a friend outside that city a mile or so and writes a letter to one in British Columbia, four cents will carry each letter, though one of them has to go thousands of miles. I believe the railways will discuss in the future this idea of the stamp freight rate whereby all freight will be put on a par to all geographical centres across Canada and to all business houses.
Centralization has taken the big factories to the larger places. Why should we who are

The Address-Mr. A. Stewart
a long distance from these factories be penalized? I am going to mention only one or two cases in particular. We have no objection to the great automobile works, we will say, in Oshawa. We in the maritimes and the people all over Canada to the extreme limits of the country support that factory. The farmers around Oshawa support it by buying automobiles, but they also receive a great deal of support by growing food to feed the employees of those factories. We in the maritimes are in a different situation, and the same thing applies farther west. If one of our farmers buys an automobile at Oshawa, what happens? He is immediately penalized to the extent of anywhere from $75 to $118, because he must pay the freight from Oshawa; whereas the farmer who lives around Oshawa get his car for that much less. I mention this in my argument that if a stamp freight rate act were in existence in this country, which it will be in the near future just as sure as we are sitting here tonight, that difference would be equalized. When the cost of that car was made known at the works, what would happen? They would say, "We are sending so many of these to the maritimes and so many to the west." They know the distance; they know the freight rates; and the freight would be added to the cost of the car. Hence, a farmer in Oshawa who gets the benefits in every way of the automobile factory there would have to pay the same price for his car as the man in Charlottetown, Prince Edward Island, would have to pay for his. That is giving fair and equal rights to all.
I might mention one other case, Mr. Speaker, if you will allow me to do so, and it is this. There is in Canada one industry, and I think it is the rubber industry, that prepays the freight. I have not been engaged in that industry for a few years, but when I was in the rubber industry they prepaid their goods to all parts of Canada. I think there was one place as to which they made a little difference, and that was away out in the Alaska territory. What was the consequence of that? Because of their stamp freight rate system, a merchant in Charlottetown could buy $100 worth of footwear at the same price in Kitchener, Ontario, as the merchant living next door to the factory.
Those are things which will have to be considered. In justice to the rest of Canada we should have this matter brought up and a study made of it by our railway system.
I am sorry that I have not time to deal with the fisheries of Canada because the fishing industry is second only to our agricultural
industry. A little later on I hope to have an opportunity to do justice to it, if I can.
One other matter I should like to mention is in connection with the mail couriers in our province, and their problems. But, since there is an item coming up in the estimates under which it can be discussed, I will postpone discussion of it till then.
May I thank you, Mr. Speaker, for the overtime.

speechtext:
I should like to devote some little time, Mr. Speaker, to a discussion of the economic situation of those who have been and are now public servants of the Dominion of Canada. We have a civil service, which is yet young and perhaps in some ways immature but potentially one of 'the best, and I am convinced that we have among the higher reaches of it public servants who are second to none in any nation of the world. Yet in the public service of Canada there is an element of unrest which is noticeable all across the dominion, particularly amongst those in the lower paid groups. So far as the public service goes, they are the ones who have been most badly hit by the drastic increase in the cost of living. From October last until now I believe there has been an increase of another ten points in the cost of living of Canadians. As I say, that an element of unrest prevails is obvious, and we can see that from the resolutions which have been sent to us from meetings of civil servants in every large city in the dominion.
Just here I should like to give a little advice which may be considered by the civil service to be gratuitous; nevertheless it might be well worth considering. They have between sixty or seventy organizations, all of which are to some extent frittering away their energies in an attempt to protect and help sipgll segments of the civil service. I think they would be far better off if they had one large organization which could conduct negotiations for collective agreements as an organization with the other organization, which, of course, is the Dominion of Canada. Because they do not have that one large organization, the smaller groups are weak and we see a situation such as that which prevails in the city of Winnipeg, where in quite a number of classifications the civil servants of our city have higher salaries than the civil servants of the Dominion of Canada.
Here are some instances. These would be corresponding jobs with the city and with the dominion. A clerk, grade I, in the city of Winnipeg, has a salary range from $1,020 to
The Address-Mr. A. Stewart

$1,560, while in the dominion civil service the range is from $1,020 to $1,380. A clerk, grade
II,	in the city of Winnipeg ranges from $1,620 to $1,980; in the dominion civil service the range is from $1,440 to $1,860. A clerk, grade
III,	in the city of Winnipeg, gets $2,040 to $2,220, while the federal government pays a person in a similar job $1,860 to $2,100. A senior clerk in the city of Winnipeg gets $2,280 to $2,460; in the federal civil service he gets $2,100 to $2,400. A principal clerk in the city of Winnipeg gets $2,520 to $2,820, while a person in a similar job in the dominion civil service gets $2,400 to $2,880. The city of Winnipeg is not notoriously rich, as those who live there realize, but it is sufficiently progressive to pay its own servants salaries which are considerably larger in many cases than those paid for similar jobs by the federal government. I think the government of Canada could well afford to take a leaf out of the book of Winnipeg and examine more closely the range of salaries paid, with the intention of raising them.
As I have said, the situation which we have today, where the policy of the dominion government has been to raise prices all across the board in Canada, has created unrest; and I am dealing solely with the unrest in the civil service. If the cost of living continues to go up, then undoubtedly the salary increase which was granted recently will be completely nullified. The suggestion I have to offer is this, and I think it is worthy of consideration. The amended salary rates as they existed at October of last year should be accepted as basic salaries. The increase in the cost of living should be compensated for by giving the civil servants a bonus to some extent commensurate with that increase. If put into effect, I believe such a plan would remove some of the unrest which now prevails and would undoubtedly be fairer to those people who are giving the best days of their lives to the Dominion of Canada.
There is one other group about which I should say something too; that is, those classified as temporary employees. Across Canada we must have thousands of civil servants who come within this category. It is unfair to those who have been working for six or seven years, or more, to find that they have no permanency at all. Indeed there are some employees of this house, I am told, who have been on a temporary basis for at least six or seven years. That is wrong. If a person is employed in the civil service I have no objection to his being given a probationary period, which I do not think should exceed one year; but, after that period, he should 
undoubtedly be given the security that comes with permanent employment. There is also one other group who work for us,-namely the sessional staff, who as yet have received no increase to compensate for the increased cost of living. I hope that very shortly increases will be announced for these loyal and faithful workers in this house.
However, there is another group, who were also civil servants at one time, whose plight I wish to draw to the attention of parliament. I refer to the superannuated civil servants who gave most of their working days to the jobs which were theirs, and who are now retired. I have in my hand sessional paper No. 22, which is a report on the operations of the Civil Service Superannuation Act for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1947. An analysis of this document is interesting. I find that, in the year it covers, some 1,100 civil servants were retired because they had reached the age limit of sixty-five. Of those 1,100, some 442 were retired on a pension of $43 a month. We have to remember that those retired on such a small pension must have been working on a small salary; and during these days small-salaried people are not able to save any money for their old age. They have to use every cent they get in the struggle to live, and they have nothing left in the form of savings to augment whatever pension they are given. How two people over sixty-five years of age can possibly hope to exist today on $43 a month is something only treasury board can tell us. I am convinced that no one else can do so.
But included in the 1,100 are 103 who have been retired on a pension of less than $17 a month. In that respect I should like to quote part of a letter which was addressed to Mr. E. E. D. Wilson, secretary of the superannuated civil servants, whose office is here in Ottawa. It concerns a lady, who for obvious reasons I shall call Mrs. X, though her name is available to anyone who would like to know it. She is a superannuated civil servant who landed in hospital in Toronto with pneumonia, of course under the care of a doctor. A friend of Mrs. X wrote the letter, part of which I am going to quote:
I might also advise you that the same doctor tells me it is from the type and kind of living Mrs. X has been trying to exist on and from what her meagre monthly superannuation cheque could provide that has brought her to the state of malnutrition and this illness; that the monthly amount she now receives of $28.87 had not provided for the necessary things of life, and this is all she has in the world-so by the time_ she paid room rent there wasn't much left for food or anything else.

The Address-Mr. A. Stewart
Some may say, well, why did she not pocket her pride and go to her friends and beg or borrow from them in order to live a little better? Those who ask that question have very little regard for the pride many people have when it comes to borrowing from one's friends or relatives or neighbours. Here is an elderly woman, over sixty-five years of age, with this meagre, pitiful pittance of $28 a month, whose doctor has diagnosed her trouble, apart from its being pneumonia, as malnutrition. And if that happened to a person receiving 828, what about those 103 civil servants who are in receipt of something less than the meagre sum of $17 a month? But I believe some 156 or 157 civil servants died while still in the service, and they left behind widows and children. One hundred of those widows average as a pension less than $30 a month from a grateful state, while the average child gets about $6. One can imagine the plight of a woman getting on in years, with a child perhaps at school and an income of $36 a month, trying to educate, clothe and feed that child as well as keep a roof over its head. It is a manifest impossibility with prices as they are just now.
Then last year some civil servants died after retirement. They left 179 widows; and of those relicts of superannuated civil servants some 121 today receive an average of about $30 a month from a grateful nation. I have a reasonable command of the English language, Mr. Speaker, but I find it very difficult to put into parliamentary language what I think of conduct such as this. However, I shall read extracts from two other letters which perhaps will point up the situation better than I can do myself. These letters also were addressed1 to the superannuated civil servants' association. Here is part of one:
My husband's pension was thirty-nine dollars and some odd cents, he barely lived three years after pension was granted and after his death, as you know, gave me half, which is $19.58, and I was more in need of if 'after his death than before.
The letter spoke of a cost-of-living bonus, and being under the doctor's care now for two years I find I cannot meet the expenses-doctor's bills, fuel for the coming winter and living expenses.
We should remember that elderly people are going to spend more money per capita for medical care than those who are younger and still working. Elderly people need more help than, they are getting today, if for no 5849-112
other reason than to provide medical care. Here is still another letter addressed to Mr. Wilson:
Dear Sir:
How that high cost of living is steadily going upward we just can't cope with my pension of $38.75 per month.
One can of vegetable soup has to be enough for the whole day. If you say that this is a living, I would rather want to be dead than alive.
You will remember, Mr. Speaker, that here I am dealing with only one small group in Canada, the superannuated civil servants, not with that vast mass of elderly people who have very little to live on. I am referring to just one group in particular, but what I have to say applies to all of them. When we think of what they have to exist on we must realize at once that their conditions are absolutely and utterly intolerable.
What has been the reaction of the government? Well, a statement was made some weeks ago by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) on behalf of the government, in which at one point he said in effect that, in comparison with industrial pension payments, the superannuated civil servants were not too badly off. The fact that industrial pension schemes are inadequate is no reason for the federal government saying that that is good enough for us, and following blindly along the way generally accepted by industry. One would hope that in the matter of employment the federal government would give a lead and not follow quite so sheep-like in the footsteps of others.
Another statement which was made was that there had been a considerable contribution by the government to the pension scheme, and that therefore it was impossible to consider giving any additional money to help these people. I cannot agree with that statement. I do not believe any contribution has been made by the federal government. I think that when the federal government paid money into this fund it was, in effect, paying part of the wages which civil servants would have got, had there been no fund. And on the basis of that argument there has been no contribution of any kind, let alone what the Minister of Finance called a considerable contribution.
It has been argued that the agreement between the superannuated civil servants and the federal government is a matter of contract. It may well be; I do not know. But I doubt it. In any event, I am prepared to argue on the basis of a contract-a contract entered into, let us say, by civil servants years
The Address-Mr. A. Stewart

ago when the general standard of pay was not nearly as great as it is today. For a certain sum of money they could buy a certain quantity of goods. But obviously the dollar of today cannot buy even seventy per cent of the goods it would buy in 1938. The government, by its own deliberate policy in taking off price ceilings, has so increased prices for the people of Canada, including superannuated civil servants, that their dollar is now vorth practically half what it was before the var. This policy has been entered into deliberately by the government, and by entering into it they have caused great harm to those who live on fixed pensions in this country.
The government's answer has been No, that it would not consider a cost of living bonus for these civil servants who are now superannuated and who have received no help whatsoever through the years of the war. The government's "no" seems to be dogmatic and categorical. Nevertheless I hope the government wall reconsider its policy. After all, we shall end this budgetary or fiscal year with a surplus gi-eater than we have ever before known. There are many over there who may take pride in accumulating as surplus hundreds of millions of dollars. They would be better advised to take pride in using that surplus to improve the conditions of people in Canada, and especially the conditions of their own servants.
There is one other matter which I wish to draw to the attention of certain ministers, principally the Minister of Trade and Commerce. These matters deal with housing in various parts of the country. I intend to read extracts from certain letters, and I shall do so in good faith, though I have not been able to investigate these conditions, myself.
I have here a letter from Mrs. E. Sutherland of Fort William, Ontario, who writes on behalf of tenants of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. She states that last July those tenants were led to believe that the government houses they occupied were for sale, but that nevertheless it would be reasonable for them to expect to continue to live in these homes on a rental basis. Then, within the last few weeks those tenants have been suddenly asked either to buy or to get out. They are to be moved somewhere else, and they have not been told where they are to be moved to. I am informed by Mrs. Sutherland that the agents of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation are using methods which

she says are creating a campaign of fear. These are her words:
These methods are . . . directed especially against the women of the household, so upsetting and terrifying them that they in turn force their husbands to buy against their will.
I do not say that is true, nor do I say it is false. It is an allegation which is made, and if it is true it is shameful. Therefore I would ask the government immediately to investigate the facts of the situation in Fort William. In some instances I am told tenants are being given from three to ten days to make up their minds as to whether or not they intend to buy these homes. I think most people who *buy houses these days are being rather reckless, not to say stupid, because value is not in the homes which are being built. Furthermore for the average worker the cost of a home today is such that he will be mortgaged for the rest of his life in attempting to secure ownership of the home. Houses are too dear. And, what is even worse, there is this dreadful insecurity on the part of tenants who feel that their present jobs may not last. Yet they are being forced by a government agency either to buy or to get out. I suggest that the situation needs immediate examination.
Then, I have some letters in connection with Wartime Housing Limited. We know that this company entered into contracts with municipalities throughout Canada. I thought, at the time those contracts were entered into, that perhaps those municipalities had put their names to improvident contracts. The municipalities would get only about S24 to $30 a year in taxes.
Now these same municipalities find that they have to supply lighting and educational as well as other facilities to the tenants of these houses. Naturally they want additional taxes. In a statement in the house a little more than a year and a half ago the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Howe) said that the municipalities would get another $2 a month per house. Unfortunately it does not seem to have stopped at $2. After all, it is not the fault of the tenants if the municipalities have entered into what conceivably in law may be an improvident contract.
Surely it is not right that this creature of the government should turn around and compel tenants to pay increased taxes which the various cities and municipalities want, At this point I quote part of a letter from St. Catharines, Ontario, stating in part:
You are aware no doubt that these homes are temporary dwellings falling rapidly into deterioration for the following reasons:	They are
built on cedar posts with no foundation; they

The Address-Mr. A. Stewart
are built of unseasoned lumber; they are built on the outskirts of the city -without proper drainage facilities.
I do not know what the facts are in St. Catharines, but I have suspected in other areas that these Wartime Housing homes were of a very temporary nature and that they might eventually become slums. Then, the letter contains the following suggestions:
Our appeal is based on the following headings:
1.	Tenants are not liable for taxes;
2.	The assessment of these properties is too high;
3.	The present rental is adequate to meet all tax requirements.
I believe that third statement is pretty accurate, and I can see no reason why the government should compel tenants to pay increases in taxes when probably sufficient rental accrues to the government to absorb the increased overhead.
Then we have a case in which the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. Sinclair) may be interested. This, too, is a Wartime Housing scheme in Vancouver. In this scheme the tenants pay about $225,000 a year in rent. Of this sum, $18,750 goes to the city in taxes. Then, $126,000 a year is allotted for administration and maintenance, and $81,000 for credit on capital account. I am told that these houses have at least had one exterior paint job and that most of them have had two interior jobs of redeeoration. Nevertheless we are faced with the fact that $126,000 for five years adds up to $630,000. And, if we assume the cost of painting and decorating to be the fanciful figure of $230,000, there is still $400,000 left, or an average of $80,000 a year to look after administration of this project. It is difficult to believe that this $80,000 a year is entirely swallowed up in administration costs. If such is the case, then obviously the administration had better be cleaned up rapidly, for it must be incompetent. But I doubt if there is such incompetence, and so it is out of the surplus which the tenants give that I think Wartime Housing Limited ought to pay the increased taxes which are asked by the city of Vancouver.
Here again I quote from a letter from Mr. J. Nuttall, secretary, wartime housing tenants committee, in which he says:
This proposed increase means hardship to many people in these homes. We can cite instances of burned-out pensioners living on $65 per month. A man (veteran of both wars) and his wife and daughter living on the daughter's earnings of $28 per week. Widows with small children receiving $50 monthly. War veterans
comprise over half of those living in these wartime homes. Names and details of these cases can be supplied on request. These people now are being presented with a new lease which states "$5 per month more to meet municipal costs" and are being forced to sign on pain of eviction from the premises. This, in our opinion, is one of the most glaring cases of callous disregard of the administration to the interests of the people.
Those may be strong words, but I rather suspect that they are well merited.
I have still another case having to do with the workers at Kenora. The information about this case was provided by the reeve of the municipality of Jaffray and Melick, who states that the workers at a local airport have been required to pay a 100 per cent increase in their rents. The matter was taken up with the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Howe), who answered in part:
There was an upward revision of the salaries of radio operators at that time, and provision was made that these men would not suffer any reduction in "take-home pay" as a result of the increased rent, other than through deductions for income tax .and contributions to the superannuation fund.
I do not know whether the right hon. gentleman realizes how supremely cynical such a . statement is. In effect it boils down to this: The workers there were given an increase in pay so that they could pay increased rents which in turn would go back to the federal treasury. On the other hand, it is possible that the increase in pay was given to provide for the general increase in the cost of living which has been inflicted on all of us. If such is the case, then obviously it is iniquitous literally to tax all the increase out of the workers in the form of increased rent.
There are one or two more things I should like- to say on housing, particularly with reference to a speech made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. St. Laurent) before the politics club of McMaster university. This is a very revealing speech indeed. The minister made clear his views on housing when he said:
I'm against subsidized housing because it would be available to a few privileged ones.
I do not know how the right hon. gentleman arrived at such a conclusion. If he has aspirations such as have been suggested in the public press I think he should become rather more familiar with the ramifications of housing in this country. Subsidized housing is designed to help underprivileged people, not the privileged ones. The submerged third of our people earn less than $1,400 a year. Those who earn such an amount of money obviously are not in a
5849-112J
The Address-Mr. A. Stewart

position, to pay the inflated prices which are asked today for new homes, neither are they in a position to pay more than $20 or, at the outside, S25 a month in rental for their families. Private enterprise today cannot and will not build houses which will renit for $25 a month. Therefore, if we are to give the submerged third of our population a chance to live in dignity and decency; if we are to get them out of the slums, obviously we have to subsidize the cost of the homes which they will inhabit. I think that is a matter which the ninister of external Effairs ought to study more dosely. Still speaking on this matter of subsi-iized housing, he goes on to say:
It would be risking temptation to put into the hands of politicians a few thousand houses which could be given to certain persons. It would be a temptation to buy votes.
I think that question comes perilously close to being a question of privilege. Of course the right lion, gentleman may know his colleagues better than I do, but I cannot think of any. member of parliament using the provision of homes merely for the purpose of buying votes. I am going to repeat what the C.C.F. has suggested with regard to a housing scheme. Having heard this, I am sure the minister of external affairs will realize that it would be impossible for a politician to give away houses as he envisages.
We suggest that there should be a housing department set up by the federal government-and that similar housing departments should be set up by the nine provinces, the federal department and the provincial departments working closely together. Working with the provincial departments there would be the municipalities and the larger zones. The municipality would- decide what homes were needed and the matter would be cleared eventually with the provincial authorities. Then the federal government would be asked to supply the money necessary to build low-cost homes all across Canada. I do not see how possibly the pork barrel which the right hon. gentleman fears could enter into such a scheme.
I am not going to discuss housing further at this moment because we shall be given an opportunity later on in the session to debate the obvious inadequacies of the government in providing homes for the people. All I say now is that I have brought certain glaring injustices to the attention of the House of Commons, particularly to the attention of the ministers concerned. I hope these injustices will be investigated and, if what I have said is true, as I believe it is, that they will be immediately rectified.

Mr. Speaker, along with my fellow members who have spoken in this debate, I hasten to offer my heartiest congratulations to the mover of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. The hon. member for Lake St. John-Roberval (Mr. Dion) has shown once again how clearly and accurately he can state his views in this house.
(Text):
I wish to congratulate the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Dickey) upon the overwhelming victory in the last by-election and upon the splendid contribution he has made to this debate. His maiden speech augurs well for a long and fruitful political career. I think it is proper also at this stage to say a few words about the changes which took place recently in the cabinet.
It was with deep sorrow that we witnessed the departure of the Right Hon. Ian Mackenzie. As a member of this house, I thank him most sincerely for the marvellous task he accomplished 'as the minister in charge of the Department of Veterans Affairs, and on behalf of the veterans of my riding and speaking for myself as well I wish him every success in his new political functions.
The new Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) also retains the portfolio of the Department of Reconstruction and Supply. Canada is fortunate indeed to have his remarkable capacities at its disposal in the present crisis. His numerous and brilliant achievements during the war as Minister of Munitions and Supply are guarantees of success for the future.
Some of our colleagues have seen fit to voice criticism of the appointment of the former Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) to the portfolio of fisheries. Representing as I do a riding where fisheries is one of the main industries, I say now sincerely that this appointment put the right man in the right place. The main, and most important, problem of our fishermen today is the difficulty in obtaining markets for their production. The minister has acquired valuable experience in this field as Minister of Trade and Commerce, which experience can do no less than benefit the industry as a whole. I assure the minister in the name of the fishermen of my riding that we are pleased to see him at the head of this department, and that he will have our unfailing co-operation.
We look also to the new Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Gregg) to carry out the good work of his predecessor, and I pray him to accept our best wishes in this new field.

Here is the first of these statements on which I want to comment. I quote textually from Le Devoir:
I note with sadness, says Mr. Chaloult, that the strongest immigration movements took place

while' a French Canadian guided the destinies of our country.
That statement is absolutely false, and I shall prove it. Mass immigration to Canada did not begin in 1896 during the Laurier regime, as Mr. Chaloult contends, but in 1871 as shown by the following statistics:
From 1871 to 1881, 362,893 immigrants entered Canada, or 90,233 more than the natural increase in population during that decade. From 1881 to 1891, 920,351 immigrants settled in Canada, that is 179,351 more than the natural increase in population during the same period.
It should be noted that in this period of twenty years, the number of immigrants admitted to Canada exceeded by 279,584 the normal increase in our population. Mr. Chaloult, however, does not mention that period, because he is well aware that a Conservative administration was in power throughout those 20 years except when the Liberals took over between 1873 and 1878 under Prime Minister A. MacKenzie.
Turning to the 1891-1911 period covering the next two decades, during which Sir Wilfrid Laurier held the post of prime minister for 15 years, we find that contrary to Mr. Chaloult's claims, our increase in population exceeded by 314,970 the number of immigrants admitted to Canada throughout those years. In the light of these figures, will Mr. Chaloult still try to claim that under the Laurier administration, immigration was carried out on a larger scale than under earlier or later governments? ,
Furthermore, I shall shortly quote figures that will show Mr. Chaloult that even in the midst of war, the number of immigrants admitted to Canada between 1911 and 1921 under a Tory administration exceeded by 396.694 the normal increase in our population. Here are the figures: immigrants, 1,472,694; natural increase, 1,076,000.
If we consider this 1911 to 1921 period, under a Conservative government, as against the 1921 to 1931 period, under a Liberal administration, with a few months interruption, we find that under the latter government, the number of immigrants was 195,710 less than the natural increase. Mr. Chaloult has thus deliberately altered the facts and I believe I have demonstrated it adequately.

The Address-Mr. Lcmglois
The second excerpt I wish to quote from Mr. Chaloult's speech is the following and again it is taken from Le Devoir. Referring still to the allegedly nefarious Laurier government, the newspaper quotes Mr. Chaloult as follows:
The scum and riff-raff from the London dockside, men with criminal records and Douk-hobors were brought to Canada at great expense, while great care was taken to eliminate any French or even Latin immigration.
If only Mr. Chaloult were concerned with telling the truth, he would have added that the Doukhobors came to Canada in 1900, it is true, but only after a precedent had been set in 1873, under a Tory government. The Doukhobors were in fact preceded by the Mennonites. Some of these had already come from Pennsylvania to settle in Ontario at the beginning of 1800, but the real immigration of Mennonites from Southern Russia began in 1873 in the west, mainly in Manitoba. The Conservative government of the day, Sir John A. Macdonald being premier, passed an order in council, P.C. 957, dated August 13, 1873, authorizing the entry of Mennonites under very special conditions. They were, among other things, exempted from military service and allowed to create their own educational system. That order in council, kept secret until 1940, created the precedent whereby order in council P.C. 2747 was passed on December 6, 1898, permitting the entry of Doukhobors under conditions practically similar. Therefore, if Mr. Chaloult can blame Sir Wilfrid Laurier for having brought Doukhobors here, he must, in fairness, add that such entry had been permitted by a former Tory government which created a precedent in favour of the Mennonites. Mr. Chaloult quoted a little later some figures relating to immigration since the end of the last conflict, mentioning, for instance, that in 1947, out of 64,000 immigrants who entered Canada, 38,000 were from the British isles. I do not know where Mr. Chaloult has taken his information, but I can say that it is absolutely inaccurate and does not tell the whole' story. To substantiate this latter assertion, I need only say that since the end of the war we have granted entry in Canada, from the British isles, to 43,447 war brides and 20,992 children born of marriages between our Canadian soldiers and British girls, or a total of 64,439. Mr. Chaloult also forgets to mention that among these wives and children there
were a good many whose husbands or fathers were French Canadians from our regiments in the province of Quebec.
Continuing his argument against the dominion government about immigration, Mr. Chaloult stated that this government had even placed planes at the disposal of Ontario's premier to speed up British immigration in this country.
This statement is absolutely false, and he knows it. As a matter of fact, Mr. Drew had chartered foreign planes to carry those immigrants to Canada. However, when told that the planes could not land on Canadian territory as a result of previous agreements, he was forced to make new arrangements through Trans-Canada Air Lines for the transport of only one-third of the immigrants he was bringing into Canada. I may add that Mr. Drew paid out of his own pocket for both the foreign planes and those supplied by Trans-Canada Air Lines. The dominion government therefore did not incur any expenses for the transportation of these immigrants.
Mr. Chaloult then blamed the dominion government for placing all sorts of obstacles in the way of French immigrants to Canada. I challenge Mr. Chaloult to quote any section of our immigration act or any departmental regulation preventing Frenchmen from coming to Canada as immigrants. Our immigration act does not discriminate either in favour of some privileged class of immigrants, or against immigrants from France or Belgium.
Moreover, immigration offices are maintained by our dominion in Paris, Brussels, The Hague and Rome for the nationals of those different countries. Mr. Chaloult would promote French immigration into Canada but remarks such as he made in 1947 when he denounced what he described as French interference with education in the province of Quebec are hardly conducive to bringing more French immigrants into this country.

I must assure the Secretary of State for External Affairs that he may rely on the full co-operation of all Quebec members. May I say to him in their name: We Canadians from Quebec are proud to have you as our leader, we are proud to fight by your side and we are sure of victory because we know that our province needs you, that our country needs you, that the whole world needs you.
