subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, although I must admit that I did not follow much of what was said by the hon. member who preceded me, I promise you that I shall not impose on your good nature, or upon the good nature of members of the house, as he has done.
Speaking as the representative of Yukon Territory, I would remind the house that Yukon is the only federal territory that has a representative in parliament. The government of Yukon is administered by a controller. He is not an elected officer; he is appointed by the governor in council of the dominion or, in other words, by the dominion government. The controller operates directly under the authority of the Department of Mines and Resources; his minister is the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Glen).
Yukon was originally part of the Northwest Territories; but in 1896, because of the importance of that part of the Northwest Territories and the great wealth that was coming out from the gold mines, this parliament by an act called the Yukon Act, created Yukon Territory. That Yukon Act is the constitution of Yukon. Among other things that constitution provides for a local legislature known as the Yukon council which has relatively the same powers as the legislature of a province. It can legislate with respect to all

The Address-Mr. G. Blajck
matters concerning property and civil rights, and anyone who knows anything of law knows the wide range of subjects those words cover.
In Yukon, as in the provinces and as here in the dominion, legislation can become law only with the assent of the controller in the case of Yukon, of the lieutenant-governor in the case of a province and of the governor general in the case of the dominion. This assent is seldom withheld, but to the disappointment of the electors and people of Yukon the assent of the controller was withheld in connection with legislation passed in recent years. That assent was withheld not because the legislation was ultra vires or beyond the powers of the council to enact; it was withheld simply because it did not suit the wishes of the controller or conform to his whims. He reserved his assent to legislation which was intended to break the bonds of dictatorship and loosen the stranglehold which an official of the federal government had on the public of that territory. Rather than see that power reduced, rather than see that power controlled, assent was withheld and the governor in council promptly disallowed the legislation.
Yukon has had a representative in parliament for forty-six years, and I would call the attention of hon. members to the fact that in forty-two years out of those forty-six Yukon has been represented by a supporter of the Conservative party. Two Liberal members represented the territory for two years each, or a total of four years. Why have the people of Yukon for the most part supported members of the opposition? It is not because the great majority were supporters of the Conservative party. Conservative candidates in Yukon, including myself, would not have been elected) had it not been for the support received from supporters of the Liberal party.
Why have the Liberals not supported their own party? It is because they resent the type of government which that party has given the territory. The two elections which Liberal candidates did win were won only by gross fraud, by the padding of voters' lists and the stuffing of ballot boxes. I know that happened, because I was there. Any oldtimer will agree with me that that is one of the reasons they have never been able to elect a member.
In those days the mining laws of Yukon were enacted by orders in council passed here in Ottawa by people who were thousands of miles away from the mines and w'ho knew nothing about mining. Those laws were subject to secret changes overnight. The mining law would be something today and something else tomorrow, and the miners up there would
not know what it was. I have seen miles of valuable mining claims banned from staking or recording by orders in council passed here in Ottawa. Then another order in council would be passed throwing the land open for locating at midnight of a certain day. That tvord would get up there to the supporters of the government, but the general public would not know anything about it until all the valuable mining property had been staked.
That is one reason why they do not send Liberal members to parliament. You would think that experience would teach the government that if they want the support, the respect and the friendship of the people of Yukon they would mend their ways. But what happened only at the last session of this parliament? At that time a grievous wrong was done to the people of Yukon and the people of the adjoining Mackenzie district. By fhe Redistribution Act the district of Mackenzie was added to Yukon, notwithstanding the unanimous protests by the people of that district. They did not want it.
How did it start? I have my own idea and I shall be glad to be corrected if I am wrong. However, I know I am not. The Minister of Mines and Resources went up to Yellowknife, that important mining camp in the district of Mackenzie, along with some of his officials. The people there told him that they had not sufficient population to have a representative in parliament, but they claimed also that Yukon Territory had never had sufficient population to entitle it to representation in parliament, that it w'as only because of its importance as a producer of wealth that representation was given. The people of Yellowknife said, "Why not give us similar representation?" They were encouraged by the Minister of Mines and Resources to expect that.
But what did they get? They got tied onto Yukon, something which they did not want. They petitioned parliament and they wrote and telegraphed the minister to stop it. They told him that they would rather remain without representation that be tied onto Yukon, an impossible combination. They asked the Minister of Mines and Resources for bread and he gave them a stone. Those people resent that. This government and the minister will find how they resent it at the next general election. The government will not get support for their party by adopting tactics like that. You cannot expect people to be grateful after that kind of treatment.
That wrong could be righted if the government wished to do it. The Minister of Mines and Resources could say to his colleagues in the cabinet, "We had better amend the act
The Address-Mr. G. Black

and do away with the addition of Mackenzie to Yukon". They could put that amendment through parliament and give those people what they want and what they should have. It is not too late to right the wrong that has been done.
What treatment have the veterans in Yukon had? It is nothing for any government to be proud of. This is the third session since the war in which I have called the attention of the Department of Veterans Affairs and the government and this house to the shabby treatment the veterans of Yukon are getting. For some reason or another the officials charged with the administration of the Veterans Land Act ruled that that act does not apply to Yukon. In the debate on the Veterans Land Act on August 1, 1946,1 quoted section 7 of the act, which can be found at page 4214 of Hansard:
The director may, for the purposes of this act,
(a)	purchase by agreement, at prices which to him shall seem reasonable, or
(b)	in any other manner acquire by consent or agreement from His Majesty in the right of Canada or from any province or municipal authority, or from any person, firm or corporation, such lands and buildings situate in any part of Canada and such other property including building materials, live stock, farm equipment and commercial fishing equipment as the director may deem necessary.
Surely that is broad enough language and wide enough wording to include Yukon when it says, "any part of Canada." You cannot imagine any informed official so ignorant as to know so little geography as not to know that Yukon is in Canada. The act says "any part of Canada", and yet they do not apply it to the Yukon. They will not apply it. In order that all doubt might be removed and the act applied to Yukon I then moved this amendment; before coming into the house that afternoon I submitted it to the minister at the head of the department and he agreed to accept it. This is the amendment:
That there be added to section 35 the following:
"The director with the approval of the minister may acquire, convey, transfer, agree to acquire, convey, transfer land in Yukon territory including land within Dawson, Whitehorse and Mayo and subject to the provisions of this act and regulations made under this act may grant to veterans residing in Yukon amounts not exceeding the amount stated in subsection
3	of section 35 of this act, such grants to be used only for the purposes enumerated in subsection
4	of section 35 of this act."

I said:
I think that will set at rest any doubts which the administrators of the act, and perhaps the minister, may have.
Then the minister, now gone to that other place for his long rest, in his own polite way said:
May I thank the hon. member for Yukon for his customary courteous presentation of his argument. He was kind enough to send me notice of his amendment late this afternoon. It is quite true that the department has been giving extensive study to the situation in Yukon. I-think, however, it is only fair to the administration that my colleagues should have an opportunity for further study of the situation. I promise the hon. member that if he will be kind enough not to press the amendment tonight we will go most carefully into the situation which he has so clearly and, to my mind, convincingly presented. It does mean, though, a departure in principle from the Veterans Land Act. It means that the grant of $2,320 is made available for urban housing in Yukon where, as my hon. friend and I know, there are not extensive tracts of land available for settlement.
As a matter of fact, that would not be a departure in principle from the act; it would be a departure from the method of administration. Yukon is not urban. The whole of Yukon and all the settlements in it are rural, and it is a rural constituency in the election. The minister then said:
As my hon. friend and I know, there are not extensive tracts of land available for settlement-
In Yukon. I say there are extensive tracts of land on which to build dwellings in which to house all Yukon veterans who wish to take advantage of the act.
The minister said further:
If the house is so minded, we had hoped to get third reading of the bill tonight. I would give my hon. friend and his constituents through him the assurance that the suggestion he lias made tonight will be given most careful consideration during the recess.
Well, he considered it until he ceased to be a member of the house. I brought it up again on March 10, 1947, and I shall not repeat it except to quote my closing remarks. Having quoted the act and advanced the rights of the veterans in Yukon, these were my last words at that session, as reported at page 1210 of Hansard:
I would regret to have to conclude that the reason why nothing has been done for the veterans in Yukon is the lack of interest on *the part of the minister, notwithstanding his promised consideration.
Lack of interest is the whole thing. They are too far away from the government. They

The Address-Mr. G. Black
have only one member to come here to bother them. There is no war on. These men are not so important to the government as they were a few years ago, and that brings to mind this rhyme of Kipling, in which he said:
For it's Tommy this, an' Tommy that, and "Chuck him out, the brute!"
But it's "Saviour of 'is country" when the guns begin to shoot;
An' it's Tommy this, an' Tommy that, an' anything you please:
An' Tommy ain't a bloomin' fool-you bet that Tommy sees!
The Tommies up in Yukon see this government; they see the unjust treatment or lack of treatment that they are getting from it, and they resent the studied callous neglect of their problems. They do not ask this government or any minister of the government for favours; they ask only what the law allows them and the same treatment that veterans in other parts of Canada get. I say it is outrageous that they do not get it.
For the moment I shall refer to the Post Office Department. In the post office at Dawson the staff consists of three men, the postmaster and two assistants. They are all war veterans, splendid men, industrious and have always the best interests of the public at heart, no matter how inconvenient it may be to serve them. Of the government employees in Yukon the employees of the Post Office Department are the most poorly paid. Why that should be I do not know. The officials in other departments of the dominion government in Yukon are paid appropriate salaries and wages. It is reported to me that some of them are even over-staffed, but the employees of the Post Office Department are certainly underpaid. Take the post office building in the towm of Whitehorse in Yukon. It is a disgrace to any government; it is properly described as a shack, almost tumbling down. The people of the town are ashamed to have visitors see it as the federal building in that town.
A couple of years ago the Postmaster General had blueprints prepared showing a magnificent structure which was to be the federal building and house the post office. At this session I asked him when the building was to erected. He said, "Oh, not for some time to come, not until labour and building materials are available." Every hon. member knows that labour and- building materials are available if they want them. Buildings are going up in- that town by private enterprise. What is the reason this building is not being erected? This may not be an election year. If it turns out to be
one they will probably start to erect the buildings, hoping to get votes in that way, but they cannot dangle a bait such as that before .the people of Yukon; they are not for sale.
Another wrong that rankles and annoys the people of that territory is the administration of the Civil Service Superannuation Act. That is the act under which contributions are made by federal government employees to a fund to which the government also contributes to build up a pension fund, a superannuation fund. The act reads:
Every person to whom this part applies-
And it applies to all the federal employees in Yukon.
-shall by reservation from his salary contribute five pe-r cent of such salary to -the consolidated revenue fund.
What is "salary" as interpreted by the act? "The salary of a contributor means regular salary paid in respect of his services, together with the value of living and residential allowance." Both these items compose his salary or remuneration. When that act came into effect as long ago as 1924 it was put up to the Department of Justice to give an interpretation and to say whether a man getting a salary of, say $1,000, plus a living allowance of $1,600, must-regard that $2,500 as his salary, as defined by the act, and pay five per cent on the $2,500 or only on the $1,000. The Department of Justice said that he must pay on the $2,500, and- he paid it and was glad to pay.
Then the time came when a little group or coterie of employees left Yukon and went where they did not get a living allowance but a straight .salary. They conceived the cunning idea of getting back the money that had gone into that superannuation fund; and-can you imagine this?-the Department of Justice swallowed itself, reversed its decision, and said that the living allowance was no part of the salary, and gave them back their five per cent from a fund they had no right to touch. After that they did not assess the continuing employees on anything but that part of their remuneration -termed "salaries," and when those employees retired and were superannuated they received a much smaller pension than they would otherwise have got and which they would have gladly bought for themselves.
That is the interpretation put on that act by the department which has the administration of retiring salaries. -But what interpretation does the Department of National Revenue put on it, where they reach out and take income tax? The whole sum of this man's pay is $1,000,
The Address-Mr. G. Black

his salary, and his living allowance is $1,500. The total is properly and correctly, by that department, termed "income," and he pays income tax on it, whereas next door the other department says it is not income at all. Can you imagine such inconsistency between two departments of government working together? It is not salary for superannuation but it is salary for the collection of income tax. And then you wonder why this government is not popular with the people of Yukon, when it uses its own employees in that way.
That is not a worn-out grievance. It is true the act was passed in 1924; but it will be a wound, an unhealed sore, as long as the government has a federal employee in Yukon Territory. As I said before, one would think the government and the ministers would learn from experience. But wffiat is happening now?
Here is one of the Yukon mining acts, an act that regulates the mining of lode gold, and it contains this provision:
7S. The recorded owner of a mineral claim shall have a survey thereof made at his own expense by a duly qualified dominion land surveyor under instructions from the surveyor general within one year from the date upon which notification by the minister to do so may be sent to him.
2.	Such notification shall not be given until the expiration of at least one year from the date upon which the claim was recorded.
3.	If the survey is not made, and if the returns of such survey are not received and approved by the surveyor general within one year from the date of notification, the entry granted for the mineral claim shall be subject to immediate cancellation in the discretion of the minister.
That section is there in the act, passed by this parliament, but it was never intended that any minister should use it in that dictatorial way. There has not been a dominion land surveyor resident or practising in Yukon for the past ten years, and I doubt -whether in the whole dominion there are 100 dominion land surveyors. The provinces own their own lands and have their own provincial surveyors, but a provincial land.1 surveyor would not have authority in that territory. It would have to be done by a dominion land surveyor, and the minister has caused these notices to be sent to these claim owners under the threat that if they do not do as the notice requires then their claims are liable to cancellation at his whim.
Take the case of a claim where the prospective purchaser can come and say to the claim owner, "Have that claim surveyed, or we will drop the option, or you will lose the claim, and if you cannot afford to survey it we will have it surveyed and cut the price in half to you."

This is the weapon which the ill-advised policy of the minister has put in the hands of the big fellow, to bully and bludgeon the little fellow, perhaps to break him, perhaps to ruin him. It should not be done, and I hope the * minister will wake up to the wrong he is doing these people and call it off. That is another reason why the government is not popular in Yukon, and I think hon. members will agree that the government should not be popular under tb.ese circumstances.
Before I leave that, I do not want hon. members to think the people of Yukon are not alarmed at this latest manoeuvre of the minister of mines. Here is a telegram that has come to me from the telegraph office of Carmacks, Yukon Territory, under date of February 18:
We the undersigned prospectors are the original discoverers of -all gold lode deposits found to date within the Mount Freegohl -and Nansen areas of Carmacks district. We hereby vigorously protest the authorization by the minister of mines of the issuing of notices to the recorded owners of quartz mining claims making imperative a survey by dominion land surveyor within one year from date of notification. -Since 1940 in spite of depression, war -and lack of governmental assistance of any nature whatsoever we have continued to develop our properties and we have collectively paid into -the recorder's office in excess of $10,000 in recording and renewal fees -alone. Placing of the Canadian dollar on a parity basis h-as put gold mining across Canada in the doldrums and has pu-t the undersigned on the rocks. This action of *the minister means certain- -ruin and irreparable loss to all the undersigned. Repeated -appeals for improvement of the glorified moose trails called roads have been met with bureaucratic -indifference and -appeals for assistance in other ways have been answered by an eloquent silence. No surer method could be devised- to drive the pioneer Yukon prospectors from the field than to enforce this ruling of the minister. Point out one single mining field in Yukon located by representatives of any mining or exploration company. Frequent requests have been made by pioneer prospectors -that there be made available copper plaques to be -affixed to claim stakes e-ach pl-aque bearing a number, etc., duly recorded in the -recorder's records thus providing a permanent -reference for all. The action secured from the territorial government on these requests h-as been nil. The undersigned feel that a true expression of the opinion of all owners of mining claims should be -arrived at through a plebiscite in Yukon before this rilling of the ministers is made effective thereby -affording an example of democracy in -action. Petitions of protest -are being prepared through Yukon. iSgd. W. J. Langh-am, E. J. Forrest, George Fairclough, P. F. Ruber, Angus McLeod, Wm. Forbes. Jack Carpenter, George McDad-a, Alf Brown. O-rloff King, John C-arlson, Frank Goul-ter, William Te-are, Karl Paulsen, Gordon Dixon.
A plebiscite! They do not realize that the minister and- the government apparently care

The Address-Mr. G. Blajzk
nothing at all for public opinion. To show that the minister knows, and his department knows, how difficult and, in fact, impossible it would be to have these surveys maide within the time limit stipulated in these notices, I will turn to a pamphlet which his department has- just issued on, the Alaska highway, giving information, and very good information, as to the situation there. Listen to this section:
Normally, public or crown lands in Yukon territory are disposed of by sale or by lease.
At the present time, however, on account of lack of surveys, only "permission to occupy'' is being given in the case of lands situated along the Alaska highway on which buildings are to be erected . . .
They cannot even get surveyors to survey their own property. How do they expect that to be done by these miners who are notified and threatened that if they do not do it within a year and have the survey accepted by the surveyor general, their claims will be cancelled?
Yukon is strictly a mining country. Gold was found there first in quantity on August 17. 1896, fifty-two years ago, and millions are still being produced. To date the production of minerals has been approximately as follow's:
Gold	 $300,000,000
Silver	 25,000,000
Lead	 a,000,000
Copper	 3,000,000

Silver mining is just getting into its stride, and, in addition to that, $30,000,000 million of silver and lead produced, within the next few years production will be trebled and quadrupled. Yukon has valuable deposits of coal, but up to date coal has not been properly mined. Realizing the shortage of fuel there, one of the mining companies put up a proposition to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Howe), who. from my experience of him, is a man of vision and of action, pointing out that they might not have funds enough to develop that coal commercially. The minister obtained particulars. He had his engineer go and look at the property. He discussed the matter with other ministers; he discussed it with me as the member representing Yukon, and he agreed to support that company with government funds until the mine came into production. I am happy to say that it is now in production and that the support which the minister offered will not be needed. They can get along under their own steam. But that incident showed vision and action on the part of the minister, and ,1 only wish that another department I know of were under his management.
Yukon imports practically everything the people use. It produces such minerals as gold, silver, lead, copper and zinc. It imports food, clothing, tools, lumber, oil and gasoline. For over fifty years Yukon has been a splendid market for Canadian goods, and it will be for untold years to come. This dominion government gets a revenue on nearly every transaction that takes place in Yukon. It collects customs dues, excise tax, sales tax and income tax. In regard to many goods imported into Yukon on which duty and tax are paid, the taxes are paid outside Yukon, for which Yukon gets no credit. Ever since gold has been mined there, this government has collected a royalty on gold, not on the net output but on the gross output; to begin with, it was ten per cent of the gross output, then five per cent and now it is two and a half per cent. No matter how much a man loses in mining his gold, he pays the government a royalty on what he takes out. In mining other minerals he pays a tax on profits; but not so on gold. Gold pays whether it wins or loses.
During the war Yukon surrendered to the dominion government, as did the provinces, the right to collect income tax; and in compensation for that, the government made grants to the provinces and for a few years made a grant to Yukon. But after two or three years they discontinued this grant. I asked them why. Just listen to the answer! Because Yukon made a profit on selling government liquor. But the profit for the territorial government was not as much as for the federal government; where Yukon made a few thousands of dollars the provinces made millions, and the federal grants to the provinces were not discontinued. Under an act passed last session the provinces get fifty per cent of the income tax collected from companies that generate electricity for sale. We have two companies generating electrical power for sale in Yukon, and Yukon does not get one cent of their income tax. It all goes to the dominion government. Those matters mount up, I think, to convincing reasons for resentment on the part of those people in the far north.
Yukon gets no adequate return for the revenue reaped from it by the dominion government. Yukon's greatest need today is roads by means of which to develop that vast country. Dawson City is probably the oldest producing placer gold mining camp in the world, and it is not by any means a ghost town. Gold is being taken out of there by the millions every year and will be for years to come, long after we have gone. In winter the town of Dawson is isolated from the rest of the
The Address-Mr. Boivin

world, except for aeroplane travel. There was a road, but the government abandoned it and let it go back to bush; I do not know why. In the winter, vegetables and fruit, and all perishables that cannot be kept in storage throughout the winter, have to be taken in to these people at Dawson by air express and at an enormous cost for transportation. A road that is needed-and I hope the government will see its way clear to have items in the estimates this year for it-is a road from the silver camp at Mayo to the port of Minto on Yukon river, so that supplies can go into these silver mining camps at all seasons of the year and so that their ore and concentrates can go out to the smelters. The reason I say that is that the only means of transportation into that camp -and you cannot haul in ore and all the supplies that are needed in mining by means of aeroplane-is by river in the summer; and it is a temperamental river that sometimes goes almost dry. As everyone knows, you cannot run a boat on dry land; you must have water. So the government should put in this road which would give transportation at all seasons of the year. Their revenue from these mines and the importance of the mining are sufficient to justify the expenditure.
The deputy minister of mines and resources honoured Yukon with a visit last summer. He looked into the problems of the people. He discussed them with the controller; he discussed them with members of Yukon council, and he agreed that there should be a firm agreement between Yukon Territory and the dominion government for a period of years providing a fixed revenue so that the territory might plan its expenditures, in the way of developments, and know it would have the money to carry them out.
I hope that visit of the deputy minister who, I am happy to say, shows an active interest in the affairs of the territory and its development, and the work he is doing on behalf of that territory will result in such an agreement being arrived at, and that Yukon will not have to come to Ottawa year after year as a mendicant begging alms, which is the position today and always has been, but that it will receive a fair return for the revenue it provides to the federal government.
(Translation):
Mr. MARCEL BOIVIN (SheffordO: Mr. Speaker, many hon. members, during the current session, have taken the opportunity afforded by the debate on the address to express their views relative to the welfare of the country and at the same time they have submitted pressing requirements of their constituencies.

I will admit I have a similar purpose in mind. However, before I deal with these two points, I wish to abide by the old parliamentary tradition and offer my sincere congratulations to the mover of the address. I will only say this: he is a master and as such he has acted in a masterly manner. I confess, Mr. Speaker, that my colleague and friend, my neighbour in this house, the hon, member for Lake St. John-Roberval (Mr. Dion) has given such a good historical outline of his constituency and present circumstances relevant thereto, he has made us so eager to see it that man}' from his group in the far right of this house are already planning to visit his district in the near future.
To the seconder, I offer my sincere congratulations, first, on account of his brilliant victory' in the Halifax by-election and then on the manner in which he discharged his duty. We all agree, I am sure, that it was for him a delicate task to address himself to this house such a short while after his arrival. I may add that the tact he showed in thanking the proposer in his own tongue pleased all the French-speaking members of this house. He may be sure that those sentiments he expressed are reciprocated by all of us. Let us hope that they are shared by everyone here, so that we may, in this way, achieve that unity which has so long been wished for.
I would like to congratulate the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) in the name of those whom I represent, and in my own, on the great honour conferred upon him by His Majesty in granting him the Order of Merit, on his recent visit to England. Let us hope that the wish expressed on January 29 by the hon. member from Bonaventure (Mr. Arsenault) may be fulfilled and that the Prime Minister may achieve this "honour which would fittingly crown his career" and of which every Canadian, regardless of political affiliation, would certainly be proud.
Mr. Speaker, I could also sketch the history of my constituency and of its county seat, Waterloo, or of its chief industrial centre, Granby. If I were to choose to recount the history of the latter I would1 have to go back to the political history of 16th centurj! England. We would find there that the origin of the name "Granby" is linked with that of a noble family, the Manners. Subsequently, as we would see, George III, ordered by a royal decree, in 1801, that the then township be known as Granby. It became a village in 1859 and a city in 1916. The present session, however, threatens to be quite long. I will leave this work of historical research to a historical society which has just recently been

The Address-Mr. Boivin
formed in that city and which may in due course publish the history of what has beoome one of the most prosperous industrial centres of Canada.
At the beginning of this session, the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) said:
We are now meeting at a. time when this country is going through a critical period of her economic history.
You will agree with me, Mr. Speaker, that every country, after a war, finds itself in such a situation. That was the chief reason why immediately after victory in Europe, the Canadian people again placed their confidence in the Right Hon. William Lyon Mackenzie King. That is all the more remarkable if we consider that after both wars, the first as well as the second, the most powerful and strongest statesmen who had succeeded in leading their nation to victory, for instance in England Lloyd George and later Churchill and in this country the leader of the Conservative party, in 1921, could not hold power in spite of all the prestige they had gained.
Moreover the Canadian people wanted thereby to express in a tangible way their admiration for the prime minister's intelligent and skilful leadership shown during the war to annihilate the subversive principles of nazism and fascism. Yes, Mr. Speaker, the Canadian people did want to be led, in these difficult years, by a government gifted with foresight which, despite criticisms, would put Canada in a better position than any other country in the world. I hope the hon. members opposite will not forget their leader's quotation and will thus co-operate in a constructive way towards Canada's progress. I also hope that some of them will bear in mind that a member does not enhance his prestige by playing party politics and repeatedly uttering non-essential statements in this house, when such utterances entail expenses to the state.
Many hon. MEMBERS: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
To follow up the remarks I made at the outset, Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank the Right Hon. the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) for his co-operation at the time house building was requested for veterans in Granby. There was a rumour to the effect that we, in Ottawa, had stalled the project. May I quote, however, from an open letter forwarded by the Canadian Legion, housing division, and published
on March 30, 1947, in a weekly newspaper of my constituency, The Granby Leader Mail. The letter was entitled "Open Letter re Veterans Housing Shows lack of Co-operation here" and I quote:
(Text):
"The city council passed a resolution on August 19 asking the federal government for houses for veterans. When the federal government offered to build at least 50 houses, the city refused to co-operate."
(Translation):
The letter, Mr. Speaker, was signed by the Canadian Legion of Granby.
I wish also to thank him for having dispatched an engineer to revise and inspect our aqueduct system. Through his action, Granby will receive a 2,000,000-gallon pump within the next few days.
It might be well to add that this pump had been purchased by the city of Granby upon being assured delivery within 16 or 20 weeks. The new apparatus will automatically protect us from the immediate danger of fire and will, for the present at least, ease the water supply situation.
I would like to repeat a request I had made to the them minister of finance in 1946 and which I now make to his successor (Mr. Abbott). Since, at that time, we had just emerged from a world war and the repatriation of our soldiers had just begun, I understood that the then minister of finance was in a rather difficult position and could hardly be expected to change his budget. Last year I repeated my request, asking for a tax exemption of 81,200 for a single man and 82,000 for a married man. At that time I stated figures in support of my argument, in the form of a budget for each of them, proving that even assuming that these exemptions were granted, both the single and the married man, the cost of living being what it was then, would be unable to live within their means.
Since the budgets of married and single men which I quoted last year are already recorded in Hansard I shall merely remind you of what I said last year, namely that the deficits which were 899 and $215 respectively will be much greater this year. I therefore ask the hon. Minister of Finance, before he introduces his budget, to grant an exemption of $1,200 to single and $2,000 to married men, and also, if possible, a basic tax reduction as considerable as the one given last year.
You will perhaps think, Mr. Speaker, that I am asking much for wage-earners, but in view of the financial surplus rf the current year, I am convinced that this is feasible.
The Address-Mr. Boivin

I should like now to thank this same minister for having maintained rent controls up to March 1949, and I hope the order in council to this effect will not be amended, because the fate of thousands of tenants would be lamentable, as they are, for the most part, wage-earners. We have deprived them - of their money in order to maintain peace and harmony. In return, it is only fair and -reasonable that we leave them their housing accommodation, at least until a more favourable date, so that they may, when this order in council is repealed, find suitable quarters at a moderate price.
I should also like to call to your attention, Mr. Speaker, a question which is being much discussed throughout the country right now, -I mean immigration. No doubt, because of the great number of unemployed, there is a disposition to talk all the more about it. I am willing to admit -that this country comprises fairly large unsettled areas which could accommodate several thousand immigrants and that an excellent way to increase our population would be to entrust them with the development of our natural resources. We therefore have an excellent opportunity to increase our population by giving them an interest in the development of our national resources. But what means have we to say that these new citizens brought in from outside are going to stay in the employment assigned to them? None whatever. I sincerely believe that they will avail themselves of the first opportunity to move into industrial centres, following the example set in the past by our own fellow citizens. Already, too many of our cities and towns are overcrowded and the coming of these immigrants will inevitably add to the unemployment and the hardships of our own people. It would be too long for me to discuss the international situation. Hon. members will admit, however, that it is none too bright. The inspection of immigrants in peace time, no matter how careful it may be, never affords complete protection, as was evidenced last year. It is up to us to take the necessary precautions and it is far better not to go too fast on a road strewn with unknown obstacles.
Mr. Speaker, the constituency I have the honour to represent in this house is just about equally divided among farmers and industrial workers. Out of a population of some 38,000 people, we have 16,059 farmers.
In previous speeches, I had the honour of informing you of the development of some of our towns. Since then, even in the smallest municipalities, prosperous industries have loomed up and continue to expand, but that

does not prevent us from noting the increasing importance of agriculture in our constituency. Before resuming my seat, I wish to say a few words on that subject.
On account of its geographical position, its climate and the nature of its soil, Shefford county is well suited to mixed farming, and stock raising, the basis of the industry, is successful due to those most favourable conditions. Just a glance at statistics, which would be too long to quote here in detail, will convince hon. members. In my constituency, there are 2.386 farms, where breeders raise 48,000 head of cattle, including 30,000 milch cows.
According to official figures, in 1946, the
stock breeders as a subsidiary undertaking produced 42,000 hogs and over 260,000 fowl. Stock raising occupies an important place in our county because conditions are ideal for that venture.
Incidentally, I might add that the recent price increase authorized with respect, to pork helped our farmers who were producing at a loss. Now, if only the price of mash were slightly reduced, production would forge ahead to the benefit of breeders and consumers.
Shefford also boasts of wide stretches of pasture ground which frequently cover anywhere from 50 per cent to 60 per cent of the serviceable area of our farms. These conditions prompted our farmers to develop the dairy industry which has become the main agricultural interest in my constituency. I do not hesitate to add that milk and butter from Shefford rank among the most important in the province as far as quantity is concerned.
Frankly, I was not surprised to learn, a few years ago, that farmers of my constituency had sought and found the best means of making this industry as profitable as possible. Thanks to their initiative, we now find in Granby an organization with a membership of some 1,200 farmers who launched a specialized industry, that of powdered milk. I know that this industry and others of the same type throughout the country depend on the shipping of at least a part of their production. They need help. I hope that they may count, as a result, on the co-operation of the department concerned in securing permits from Ottawa.
I am in complete agreement with the farmers of Shefford, Mr. Speaker, as to the necessity of supplying our domestic market first. Nobody in my county would like to see

The Address-Mr. Boivin
the workers of our towns or any other class of citizens suffer from the lack of bread or butter. But you will admit nevertheless that it is our duty to maintain a good market for our farm products. While we must strive to meet local demand, it is most important that we do not allow this market to reach the saturation point.
Under normal conditions, our dairy production has been equal to our needs for many years, and in order to increase it, the establishment I have just mentioned has secured the services of an expert who has the confidence of the farmers and has justified that confidence by increasing that industry's production within a very short period. That industry therefore took on added importance. Hon. members will admit that due to a late season and a most unusual drought during the summer, our 1947 crop has been a failure. Yet, we experienced no milk or butter shortage.
Incidentally, may I say that I would be sorry should the production of margarine be allowed in Canada. I intend to prove that we have in this country enough butterfat to satisfy national demand. Shefford county alone produced in 1947 an estimated quantity of 125 million pounds of milk. The powdered milk industry has used only 36 million of these and even in 1948 when it will need 50 million pounds there will be left a balance of 75 million pounds, without taking into account the already noticeable increase in production. Because of these factors, the farmers of my constituency in their own interest, of course, but also in the general interest of our Canadian economy have decided to fulfil a patriotic duty by varying their production in order to stabilize the market and avoid surplus production.
I repeat, Mr. Speaker, that it was for the common good that the farmers acted that way. We should congratulate them and help them. I urge the government to revise the matter of export permits, which is most important to agriculture. Such a step would be in the general interest, because the farmer's prosperity is the merchant's wealth, according to an old saying.

speechtext:
This matter is not only important to my constituents but to all Canadian farmers, because, as has been stated previously, small industries of that kind are to be found everywhere in the country.
I would like to see stock breeding become the basis of our agricultural industry in eastern Canada, as the whole of our grass producing country would benefit. From a logical point of view that is the course we should take. The western provinces can supply us with the grain we need, but on the other hand we must help the western farmers and enable them to sell the surplus of their products on foreign markets, because that surplus would only lower prices and discourage that splendid movement which will not only permit agriculture to subsist, but will make for its progress.
Harmony between the various branches of agriculture is essential. Dairy farming is the basis of the industry, as it supports the production of hogs and poultry, which are needed to fulfil our agreements with Great Britain.
Now, Mr. Speaker, would it not be in order to consider how important it is to help those industries whose object is, I believe, to promote the development of basic agricultural production in this country. In fact, powdered milk has the additional advantage of furthering the improvement of hog and poultry breeding and helping supply Canadian consumers with essential commodities such as butter and cheese. Powdered milk also prevents overstocking of the market since it is in great demand abroad. Exports of this commodity therefore help maintain the price levels of our dairy products at home. Thanks to the information supplied by the wonderful organization functioning on behalf of poor children in Europe and to the particulars furnished by an official of this industry in my constituency who has just returned from Europe, we know the needs of the countries that were devastated by war. Would it not be a charitable deed to come to the help of these stricken people? To that end, we must promote exports of this commodity on the largest possible scale.
In concluding, may I repeat, Mr. Speaker, that the farmers of my constituency, as all other farmers who have estal dished this industry in other parts of Canada, have broken

new ground in this field not only in their own but in the public interest. I believe, Mr. Speaker, that they deserve our encouragement.
